subtopic: RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT AND CHAIRMAN OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS-APPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON
RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT AND CHAIRMAN OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS-APPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make concerning the office of chairman of the board of directors and that of president of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. R. C. Vaughan, who has been president since 1941, and chairman of the board of the Canadian National since 1942, reached the normal retiring age in December, 1948, but, at the request of the board of directors and with the approval of the government, consented to remain in office until such time as a successor was appointed. It is with deep regret that I announce to the house the retirement of Mr. Vaughan from the post of chairman of the board and president of the Canadian National Railways, to take effect as of January 1, 1950.
There is no need for me at this time to remind the house of the most loyal services performed by Mr. Vaughan, not only to the Canadian National Railways, with which he was closely associated since its inception, but also to the whole of Canada. In the summer of 1939 the government appointed him chairman of the defence purchasing board in Ottawa. All Canadians will recall the numerous problems that had to be solved at that time in order to prepare industry for the war effort, and the defence purchasing board was the first agency on which this responsibility was placed.
In appreciation of his distinguished services, not only with the government, but for his guidance of the largest transportation system in Canada during the war years, Mr. Vaughan, in 1946, was made a Companion of the Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George.
Mr. Vaughan, when he retires at the end of this year, will terminate a career entirely devoted to transportation. He will have completed fifty-one years of service, having been successively with the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Northern Railway, and the Canadian National Railways. His first official appointment was in 1910 as assistant to the vicepresident and general manager of the Canadian Northern Railway. He became vicepresident in charge of purchases and stores and steamships of the Canadian National in 1920. He was appointed president in 1941, and chairman of the board in 1942, at a time when the Canadian National Railways, along with the other railways in Canada, were called upon to transport men and materials in quantities unheard of before in the history of our railway transportation system. This house will agree with me when I say that our national system, under the guidance of Mr. Vaughan, contributed in no small measure to the great achievement made by Canada during the war. My colleagues in the cabinet and the members of this house will, I am sure, join with me in extending to Mr. Vaughan our very best wishes for happiness and peace of mind for many years to come.
By virtue of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1936, the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways have appointed Mr. Donald Gordon to replace Mr. Vaughan as president of the railway company, and the governor in council has today approved their selection and has also appointed Mr. Gordon chairman of the board of directors, both positions effective January 1, 1950.
I would like to take this opportunity to say the government is most gratified that Mr. Donald Gordon has accepted the invitation of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways and of the government, to assume the heavy responsibilities of these positions. Mr. Gordon is, of course, well known to most of the members of this house. His wartime services as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board made his name a household word throughout Canada, and gave him as well an international reputation. He was a key figure in the mobilization of Canada's economic resources in war, and played a leading administrative role in the subsequent orderly transition to a peacetime economy. In these great tasks, and also in his position of deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon has had a wide experience and an intimate knowledge of Canada's financial and economic affairs, domestic and international, in addition to which he has been in close working contact with the day to day problems of industry, labour and agriculture. His qualities of leadership, his gift for organization, and his ability to inspire

speakeroldname: Mr. Clarence Gillis (Cape Breton South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 60, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (enforcement).

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This bill is the same, word for word, as Bill No. 20 which I introduced in the last parliament. It has for its purpose the changing of sections 43, 44, 45 and 46 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. As the act now reads, when employers and employees bring a dispute before the board, the only power it has is to sit and listen. If the dispute between the two parties cannot be resolved, the board is powerless to do anything except let the parties go back to fighting it out on the streets. This happened, for instance, in the Canadian seamen's union strike.
By this proposed change, if two parties came before the board with a dispute the board would have the authority to determine which party had committed an infraction of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The board would be empowered to declare one or the other of the parties guilty and then turn the matter over to the magistrate's court. Whatever penalty this act empowered the magistrate's court to impose would be imposed by that court. This amend-
[Mr. ChevrierJ
ment would give the board some legal authority, and create respect for it in the minds of those who would be taking disputes before it.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
At its last sitting the committee was considering clause 3, to which Mr. Fulton had moved the following amendment:
Subject to any enactment of the parliament of Canada or the legislature of any province in exercise of their respective powers, the Supreme Court of Canada shall be bound by the law as declared in all orders of His Majesty in council hitherto made on the advice of the judicial committee of his privy council and in the reasons assigned therefor by the said judicial committee, in so far as the said law is applicable to Canada.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
There are just one or two further observations I wish to make in connection with this amendment. They arise out of remarks which have been made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice.
I believe it would be useful if the attention of the committee and of the country were directed to the fact that, in their apparent haste to press this bill through to its conclusion early in this session, the government, through the two hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred, have taken an extraordinary position with respect to the recommendations made by the Canadian Bar Association. We have seen the deliberations and recommendations of that responsible body treated with scant respect. I am not inclined to question the fact that the government had recently been returned with a substantial majority.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
That statement apparently meets with the approval of some hon. gentlemen in the house. But, as has been pointed out, that majority is not going to vanish over-

night. It is going to last presumably for five years or at least for four years. None of the gentlemen I see in the house shows any sign of illness. Therefore I think the request that the matter be treated with due deliberation is one which is logical and reasonable. That was the initial request made by the bar association. The second request was for a guarantee-I do not think it is going too far to call it that-of the principle of stare decisis, and that is the matter which we are debating in this amendment. But even that request of the bar association has been treated with little respect by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, and one other government spokesman to whom I shall refer. The Prime Minister went so far as to say that the comments of the president of the Canadian Bar Association were not within that gentleman's right or province to make. I will read the remarks of the Prime Minister as reported at page 530 of Hansard of October 4. When the right hon. gentleman's attention was drawn to the fact that although the resolution passed by the bar association did not call for the incorporation in the bill of any provision which would in words preserve the principle of stare decisis, the president of the bar association had specifically said that the resolution, in the light of the discussions which had taken place, did intend that such a provision should be incorporated in the measure, the right hon. gentleman used these words with respect to the statement of the president of the bar association:
I submit with all respect that no one man, whatever be the position he occupies in the Canadian Bar Association, and I have occupied the office of president of that association-in my day-has the right to enlarge or modify the terms of the resolution adopted by that association.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Temiscouata say "hear, hear," because we now know where he stands. I must confess I found it rather difficult to follow his remarks in this connection on an earlier occasion.
Here we have the responsible head of the Canadian Bar Association, who was present when the resolution was passed, making the statement to which I have referred. Who, may I ask, is entitled to comment on the meaning of that resolution if it is not the president of the association? Are we to take it that this subject is so sacred, and the wishes of the government majority so overpowering, that no one in this committee or in the country has the right to comment on this matter? That is the effect of the position taken by the Prime Minister. He questions the propriety of the president of the bar
Supreme Court Act
association saying what was intended by that resolution. I draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that the president of the bar association has left no doubt as to what he takes to be the meaning of the resolution. Af*er the discussion in the house had begun, he made a statement in Saint John, New Brunswick, as to the meaning to be attached to the resolution. He was reported in the press of September 28 as follows:
Though it is the practice for the supreme court to abide by the rule of stare decisis, Mr. Carter said, it is not bound inflexibly to do so. Such an enactment by parliament would safeguard provincial and minority rights, he said.
The enactment to which the president of the bar association had reference was one along the lines of the amendment which we are discussing here today. I believe it is incumbent upon this committee to consider and attach the greatest weight to the words of the responsible president of the Canadian Bar Association in discussing the meaning of the resolution which that association passed.
In the bill now before the house, Mr. Chairman, there could not be anything much less than there is now. What we have before us in the clause under discussion is a simple enactment that the Supreme Court of Canada shall have final and exclusive ultimate jurisdiction in respect to all cases arising in Canada. There could not be a much simpler declaration than that appeals to the privy council are abolished. It is not embroidered; it is without qualification. Therefore the resolution of the bar association must have had some meaning. If you take the simple proposition that appeals to privy council are to be abolished, that is what we have before us, and the bar association passed a resolution with respect to that proposition. I submit, sir, that they must have hoped that that resolution would be given some practical significance in the measure which is being considered. The only way in which that can be done is by some modification of the provisions of this bill. Having regard to this fact, taken in conjunction with the statement of the responsible president of the association that he thinks it desirable or essential that some such provision be incorporated in the legislation, I submit that this committee should give it the most serious consideration, and I suggest it is less than proper to say that the president of the association had no right to use these words or to enlarge in any way upon the meaning of the resolution.
As I have said, we have had that suggestion from the Prime Minister; we have had criticism of the Canadian Bar Association, ranging from the one expressed by the right hon. gentleman all the way down to the one

Supreme Court Act
expressed by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond on October 4, as reported at page 533 of Hansard, where, dealing with the resolution of the bar association, he is reported as having said:
I want to say that, so far as section (g) is concerned,-
And he was referring to section Cg) of the resolution.
-in which it says the rule of stare decisis ought to continue to be applied with respect to past decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada, a great deal of effrontery was shown by the committee of that organization in passing this resolution.
Here again we have the suggestion to which I have referred, namely, that this matter is somehow so sacrosanct, and the desires of the government majority in this house are so sacred, that the responsible body of the bar association, amongst whose members are numbered a great many judges, is "showing effrontery" when it even dares to deal with the subject matter of this resolution. It is a most extraordinary suggestion. If there were nothing else, that very attitude would be sufficient justification to make us pause and ask ourselves whether there is not something behind all this which it would be well for us to look into.
In fact I think there is a great deal behind it. One can gather what is behind it when one remembers the attempt which has been made again by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice to suggest that anyone who supports this proposed amendment must lack confidence in the Supreme Court of Canada. By this means, an attempt is made to whip up prejudiced feelings in support of the government's position and against the suggestion that the amendment be viewed on its merit. With respect, that is one of the most illogical positions I have ever seen the right hon. gentleman take. It is most illogical for him to attempt to distort the plain meaning of the words of this amendment out of their context and to read into them an expression of want of confidence in the Supreme Court of Canada. For him to say that those who would vote in favour of this amendment thereby indicate their lack of confidence is as illogical as it would be for me to say that those who are opposed to the amendment oppose it in fact because they do not want to see the Supreme Court of Canada bound by the rule of stare decisis.
When one observes the vehemence of the attempt to arouse prejudice which is displayed by the government, one wonders whether in fact that is not the motive behind their opposition to this amendment. I know we have the greatest verbal tributes paid to the principle of stare decisis, and we have the utmost assurance, in words, that the Supreme Court of

Canada will of course always follow that principle. But when it comes to the simple fact, Mr. Chairman, of a request to incorporate that provision in the statute, we find hon. gentlemen opposite saying "Oh, no; we cannot go that far, because it would be an expression of want of confidence in the Supreme Court of Canada." You know, Mr. Chairman, as well as every other lawyer in this committee and a good many laymen as well, that courts in interpreting statutes interpret only the words in the statutes; they even look at what the Prime Minister may have said with regard to the intention of the government when the legislation was enacted.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: That is a wrong judgment of the privy council.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: It is not.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: That Hansard could not be quoted before the court.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: No, it cannot be.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: It was decided by the privy council, and it is a bad judgment.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: We all know what the hon. gentleman who has just spoken thinks about the privy council, and I do not think the interjection need be dealt with. But the hon. gentleman knows as well as I do, and as well as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice know, that the established rule of law is that, in interpreting statutes, the courts look only to the words of the statute.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: That is one of the silly judgments of the privy council.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to use those words, he is by that very use condemning all the courts in Canada and putting them all in the same category.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Because they follow the jurisprudence of the privy council, that silly court.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I know it is beyond me to deal with the wit and wisdom of the hon. member for Temiscouata; therefore I shall confine myself to the fact that every court in Canada follows that rule; and, quite apart from the principle of stare decisis or anything else, it is the rule of law which is followed by the courts in interpreting statutes.
As a responsible legislative body if we want to make perfectly clear the laws we wish the Supreme Court of Canada to follow in exercising what is to be their new and enlarged jurisdiction as the ultimate and final court of appeal, I submit we have no alternative but to make it clear what we mean by voting for the amendment which is now before the committee.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Would the hon. member be kind enough to tell the committee what is the link between the privy council and the Supreme Court of Canada as it is now?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by that term. Perhaps he would be good enough to enlarge upon it.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: It is the woolsack. It is a bag of cotton covered with cloth, and it is put in front of the Speaker's chair in the Senate at the time of the opening and prorogation of parliament. The judges sit on it, like urchins. Some of them face His Excellency the Governor General, while the others turn their backs on him. But they sit on the woolsack because it was done in England in the middle ages. The privy council sit on the woolsack-indeed we should have a woolsack here in the House of Commons, and we should sit on it, so that the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops might sit at opposite ends, each with his back to the other.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Not so long as this government is in power.
Mr Pouliot: No, because those who sit on the woolsack are not supposed to take part in the deliberations; therefore while sitting on the woolsack they would not keep their minds in such a state of effervescence as to deliver unforgettable orations.
I am glad my hon. friends are smiling; it shows they have a greater sense of humour than I expected them to have. I want them to ask the Clerk of the Senate to take them to the attic of the Senate so that they may brush away all the cobwebs and look at that bag of wool before it is all eaten by the moths. They might sit on it, just to see what it is like to be lord chancellor.
The woolsack has such importance in the history of the British parliament that the position of lord chancellor is sometimes described as the woolsack. Occasionally they refer to the lord chancellor in terms of the bag of cotton on which he sits. I find, sir, that it is a tremendous joke; and the first thing to do, as soon as this bill respecting the supreme court as a final tribunal is passed, is to dispense with the woolsack and to let the moths eat it completely. If my hon. friends want to see it they will have to rush to the attic of the Senate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been a member of the Canadian Bar Association for many years, and as such it was my privilege and pleasure this year to attend the meeting at Banff. Banff is a delightful spot, and despite the seriousness of the profession there seemed to be a certain lightheartedness and frivolity in connection with what took place.
Supreme Court Act
On the golf course, while teeing off during session hours, I noticed a number of learned gentlemen teeing off ahead of me, some of whom were members of His Majesty's bench. Therefore I suggest it is fair to say that the frivolity at the convention was not confined to the minor satellites of the profession, such as myself, but applied generally.
I believe all who attended the Banff convention enjoyed it to the full. speechtext:
I happened to be out of the house and I did not hear the text of the amendment, but I understand that it refers to the application of the principle of stare decisis. That is a principle of law; it is not an act of parliament. The amendment seeks to have this principle read into the section. A very large body of public opinion in this country favours this amendment, and believes it would save this country a great deal of trouble in the future. The principle of stare decisis would apply to the decisions which have been given so far by the privy council.
I remember raising this question when I first entered the house in connection with two cases before the privy council. It is difficult to deal with this problem without having it sent to a committee. We on this side of the house have adopted a consistent policy in this regard. This is something which should be decided by the high court of parliament under the British constitution which we have had in this country since 1791, or as much as was applicable to our circumstances. This whole question is still before us.

This doctrine of law should be applied in the manner indicated by the amendment. I am not discussing the principle of the bill, because, as I see it, the principle of the bill is written into the amendment. So far as I can see, there is very little legal principle in the bill. I am not speaking personally because I have a great deal of respect and admiration for the Prime Minister and the way in which he has conducted the business of the house. No one has a higher opinion than I have of the Prime Minister.
As I say, this doctrine should be written into the statute. I can find little principle in the bill-legal, political or otherwise. It must be realized that for many years the judicial committee of the privy council has been enforcing doctrines of law, especially where they are founded on contract.
I remember two decisions of the privy council in connection with which I played a humble part. We should hold fast to the principles of our faith and be strong when we consider this amendment. What is more sacred than a contract? A contract between individuals can be enforced, and a nation is only a collection of individuals. There should be some method of enforcement as between nations.
We of the opposition have taken a consistent stand on this bill. We should stand firm on the principle that the state exists for the individual and not the individual for the state. This particular proposal interferes with the liberty of the subject; it encroaches on his rights and privileges. It should be scrutinized first by a legal committee. Both the bill and the amendment should be sent to a committee and I wish the minister would give his consent to that. Then we would not have to thresh out these legal problems in the house.
I believe I represent a large body of public opinion in the country. All I have said this afternoon has been based on the law of contracts; and what is the contract here? It was made at the time of confederation. If you want to treat the whole contract set forth in the British North America Act as a scrap of paper, and rewrite it, then write it for the living and not for the dead. If we are to have a new bill, let us have a proper legal measure which will have some regard for the law and the decisions of the privy council, which are binding under the doctrine of stare decisis.
This bill and these amendments should go to a committee, because in my view the decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council have protected not only minorities but majorities as well. They have been defenders of the faith, as it were, since the setting up of the contract under the act in the first place. To upset the whole thing now would be a grave mistake. A large
Supreme Court Act
body of opinion, including three former ministers of justice and attorneys general, has been opposed from the beginning to any change of this kind.
In my opinion there is very little to this bill, and as far as I can see it is not founded upon fact, nor does it include the protection for which I have asked. I do not know why these things are brought up at the present time. What is the rush to put through this legislation? There seems to be a great hurry to pass it, though we have nine or ten other matters awaiting our consideration. I can see no reason at all for not letting this bill stand for a few months, so that it may be properly considered and digested by the judges, the bar associations, and many other bodies. This is separatism in its worst form. It would lead to the disruption of the whole British empire.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
This discussion has been
largely confined to members of the legal profession in the house. I do not profess to be learned in the law, but it seems to me that in dealing with these legal matters we are rather losing sight of important aspects of this problem. I believe it is right and proper to give due consideration and some weight to the opinions of such an organization as the Canadian Bar Association, just as we give consideration-though, I may add, usually not as much-to the views expressed by such organizations as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the national labour bodies. But having given consideration to those opinions, this house must come to a final decision as to what shall be done.
I have listened to the discussion on this question of stare decisis, and to me it seems that to accept it unreservedly would place this country and its judiciary in something of a strait-jacket.	In my reading of the
British North America Act and the discussions preceding the adoption of that act in 1867, the fathers of confederation thought of it in the way that was described by Lord Sankey in 1929-which, I may add, is quoted in an excellent speech, which I think hon. members should read, by the late Hon. C. H. Cahan before the Canadian Club of Toronto on September 15, 1937. I do not know of a clearer exposition of the problem before us than can be found in the speech made on that occasion by one who had been secretary of state in the Bennett administration. The expression Mr. Cahan quoted then, which incidentally is also quoted by MacGregor Dawson in his book "Constitutional Issues in Canada, 1900-1931", was this:
The British North America Act planted in Canada a living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits.

Supreme Court Act
Then Mr. Cahan added this comment:
But that dictum has been arbitrarily repudiated by more recent decisions of the judicial committee, which have confined our constitution in a strait-jacket of their own making, and thus precluded the possibility of our Canadian constitution being developed in the future by judicial decisions, in accord with the clearly expressed intentions of the Canadian statesmen who framed the first British North America Act.
It seems to me that is a cogent paragraph, and the opinion expressed therein should be considered by this house in dealing with the proposed amendment. In very much the same connection, in the volume by MacGregor Dawson, to which I referred a moment ago, there is a quotation from an article by George F. Henderson in the Canadian Bar Review for November, 1929, at pages 617-619, in these words:
Under ordinary circumstances, a criticism of a judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council is inadvisable, but a recent decision of that tribunal, in Edwards et al v. the Attorney General of Canada et al, has attracted so much attention and has led to so much press criticism of the Supreme Court of Canada that proper respect for the administration of justice in Canada demands examination and comment.
Then he adds these words:
Probably the first thought that will occur to one who makes a careful study of the two judgments is that while the supreme court, like the House of Lords, is a court of law, subject to all the restrictions which that fact implies-
Then these are the words to which I wish to direct attention:
-the privy council is a committee advising the sovereign, not bound to follow precedent nor to determine matters presented upon grounds of law alone, but entitled, if not obliged, to advise on grounds of public policy, and to take into account matters of political expediency. Indeed, the privy council does not consider itself bound by its own previous decisions; nor do English courts regard judgments of the privy council as authoritative.
If that is so, it seems to me that any attempt to fasten upon Canada the past judgments of the privy council would defeat the very objective the fathers of confederation had in view at the outset-the planting of a living tree capable of growth and development in the future. In spite of the learned discussion we have had from hon. members on this side of the house, and having due regard to the opinions of the bar association, I do not think we should tie the hands of our judiciary by adopting the kind of amendment that has been moved by my hon. friends of the Conservative party. I speak only as a layman, but as a layman I believe that sometimes the law has been made to bind the hands of progress, and interpretations have been given which have interfered with the progress and welfare not only of our own country but of many other countries as well. I certainly think the house should vote

against this amendment and leave the hands of our own court free, confident that previous decisions involving the rights of our people will be given due consideration.
If we look over the judgments of the privy council-and this is why I cannot understand the attitude of people in some parts of Canada-we find that it has not been a protector of the rights of either majorities or minorities. This can be verified by a reading of certain decisions of the privy council. I am not going into them in detail, but I should like to draw attention to them, as quoted in MacGregor Dawson's volume from an article by Professor F. R. Scott dealing with the judiciary, beginning at page 347. As a layman I cannot see the sense of this house agreeing with some of the members of the legal profession who have spoken and who would tie the hands of the judiciary in the manner suggested by the amendment.

I believe this matter has been sufficiently discussed, and I should not be saying a word now if it were not for the remarks just made by the member for Rose-town-Biggar. Because those remarks have not very much weight, I shall be brief.
In the first place, this amendment has nothing to do with the question of abolishing appeals to the privy council. The principle of the bill was adopted by the house on second reading. The amendment has relevancy only on the basis that the house has decided to abolish appeals to the privy council.
My friend talks about trying to put the Supreme Court of Canada in a strait-jacket, as though that were to be the effect of the amendment. After hearing the hon. member's remarks, all I have to say is that if his view reflects the lay mind of this house, as he seems to suggest, then the matter is not clearly understood. It is apparent from what the hon. member has said that he does not understand the issue.
The member for Rosetown-Biggar seems to believe that the attitude of those who are opposing the amendment is that they are leaving the Supreme Court of Canada free, not bound by past decisions of the privy council. Certainly that is not the view of the Prime Minister, nor is it the view of the Minister of Justice. The argument advanced by them was that the doctrine of stare decisis is binding on the Supreme Court of Canada. This would mean that all those past decisions of the privy council are binding on the Supreme Court of Canada, whether or not such an amendment is adopted. Let us not have any empty talk, Mr. Chairman, about the effect of defeating an amendment such as this being to remove the shackles from the

Supreme Court of Canada. When it comes to an opinion on that point, as between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice on the one hand, and the member for Rose-town-Biggar on the other, I prefer the view of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. In the plainest of terms they said that in their opinion the principle of stare decisis applies and will bind the Supreme Court of Canada in the future with respect to past decisions of the privy council. If that is putting the Supreme Court of Canada in a strait-jacket, then certainly it is the view of the government that the strait-jacket should remain.

Because I do not think it is as clear as the Prime Minister and Minister of Justice contend. We do not wish to leave a matter of this vast importance to doubtful disputation after the event. This amendment is intended to settle the question. If we are to take this important step, Mr. Chairman, I think all hon. members ought to be quite clear about the argument. The argument advanced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is that, in principle, the Supreme Court of Canada ought to be free to disregard past decisions of the privy council in relevant matters. I ask every member of this house who adopts the view of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to go to his constituency and say it is his opinion that the Supreme Court of Canada should be free to disregard the decisions of the privy council in those important constitutional cases in which the privy council has made decisions of the most far-reaching importance to all Canada. If	hon.	members feel	they	do	notwant the principle of stare decisis applied, let	them	go the whole	way	and	say
that in future the decisions of the privy council upon which rest the fundamental rights of the provinces should not bind the Supreme Court of Canada. That would leave the supreme court free to rewrite those decisions, and in that way recast the constitution.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, thinking about what has been said, I would say that a layman is surely not the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.

It is not my intention to cover ground that has already been covered in this debate. The matter has been well argued in the house, particularly by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and those favouring the amendment. The amendment simply means that those who have moved it feel that the Supreme Court of Canada is likely to depart from the
Supreme Court Act
decisions of the privy council; that is a summary of it. It is conceded by those who support the resolution that in the past the Supreme Court of Canada has followed the decisions of the privy council. I asked the hon. member for Kamloops what he was afraid of, but so far he has not told me.
Since the Supreme Court of Canada has followed the decisions of the privy council, where is the necessity for this amendment? My hon. friends say there are two reasons for it. They seem to be afraid that the supreme court might not follow that practice in the future, although it has in the past. At the head of this government there is a responsible lawyer, a man in whom the bar of this country has absolute faith. After this bill is passed and the Supreme Court of Canada is strengthened, you will see that the court will follow the past decisions of the privy council and will earn the confidence of all.
Those who are supporting the amendment say that if we do not pass it we shall not be following what the Canadian Bar Association adopted at its convention. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the Canadian bar did not say that the requirements to follow the principle of stare decisis should be made a part of the law. I believe the remarks of the member for Kamloops with regard to the member for Parkdale were very unfair. The member for Parkdale was at the convention, but the member for Kamloops was not. I cannot understand why he should question what the member for Parkdale said about the convention. The Prime Minister and many other members of this house have been members of the bar for many years. I am a past president of the bar society of Saskatchewan. Most of us have been attending these conventions for a long time. I have complete confidence in what the member for Parkdale has said with respect to what happened at that convention.
I believe the subject has been discussed more fully in this house that it was at the Canadian bar convention. Having been one of the benchers of our law society, I believe it to be the duty of hon. members who are lawyers to act as members of this house and not as carrier pigeons for the Canadian Bar Association or any other association. We sit in this house as representatives of a constituency. I sometimes think the dignitaries in the Canadian bar and other associations might do well to run as members of parliament. It would be an education for some of those gentlemen who have sat in positions of safety for the last few years and attended bar conventions. They are the people who tell the legislators what their duty is.

Supreme Court Act
I do not see any real object behind this amendment, Mr. Chairman. If all hon. members supporting the amendment were as frank as the member for Parkdale, they might say: We do not believe in this amendment at all; we still believe in appeals to the privy council, even if it costs Canadians more money and demonstrates that Canadians cannot run their own courts. But instead of saying that, they introduce an amendment which, in effect, does nothing more than say that the proposer does not trust the Supreme Court of Canada. I am opposing the amendment.

We now come back to section 1, which had been allowed to stand. To section 1 we have an amendment by Mr. LaCroix, who moves that clause 1 be amended by adding at the end of section 4 the following words:
Provided that four of the puisne judges be chosen among the candidates proposed by the lieutenant governor in council, and that one of the four above-mentioned judges be chosen among the candidates proposed by the lieutenant governor in council of the province of Quebec, each province having to propose at least three candidates.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish to offer opposition to this first section. For a population of eleven million you are now going to establish a large court which will cost the country a considerable sum of money, having regard to the various officers we are going to have in that court. According to section 1 we are to have the same number of judges in our supreme court as has the United States, with a population of 127 million to 130 million. For what purpose? Who is asking for this proposal? The bar association has not asked for it. The provinces have not asked for it.
As I pointed out on another occasion with regard to this section 1, you are proposing to establish a system. In my opinion, we have no power by statute law to force this system on the country, without any consultation with the bar association or with the attorneys general of the provinces. Who is asking for this proposal? There are to be nine judges appointed; $25,000 a year is to be paid one of them and $20,000 is to be paid the others. I can tell the committee that this proposal

has not the confidence of the country at large. I should like to find out from the present minister who are the people that are asking for this amendment. What provinces are asking to enlarge this court and to pay the judges $20,000 a year? They should start at the other end and pay increased salaries to the judges who are out on circuit all over the country trying murder cases, cases concerning property and civil rights, and so on.
This particular section is one that will take away-what? It will take away from the court of last resort appeals of grace. They say they have the power; but merely because they say so does not make it so. Four former ministers of justice were opposed to this change. They are four of the most eminent lawyers the country ever produced. One was Sir Allen Aylesworth, who was a former minister of justice. He is probably the ablest lawyer the country has produced. As I said the other day, I remember going into the court of appeal in Ontario where he had the whole docket to himself on appeals. He acted for the government in the Bering Sea arbitration. Many members of the house graduated from the Osgoode Hall law school, including the leader of the opposition, who is an able lawyer. My good friend to my right, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, was at the law school there, and many others such as Sir Edward Beatty of the C.P.R. and Sir Thomas White. The present deputy minister of justice, and he is an extremely able one, and others were graduates of this particular school. While I have great respect for my friend the leader of the C.C.F., and for the other leaders in the house including the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, there are certain definite concrete principles which I support. I cannot be blamed for that. I have always had the courage to stand up in the House of Commons for certain principles, ever since I entered it. If I have to forsake those principles, I shall have to consider whether I ought to belong to the House of Commons any longer.
I wish to say a word to the younger members of the party to which I belong and to those on the government benches today. There are many young men of great ability in the legal profession on the government benches today and in the House of Commons, and they come here at considerable personal sacrifice. Let me ask them this question. Who has asked for this legislation? How can you justify these salaries of $20,000 and $25,000 to judges who never go out of the city of Ottawa, who can live here, who can get away for several months a year, and who have only three or four terms a year? There is difficulty in getting before them. During the second war 160,000 orders in council

were passed and only four of them ever reached the Supreme Court of Canada on appeal. How many people got as far as Ottawa? Nobody could afford it. They could not afford to come away down here to Ottawa.
If the court is to be the kind proposed by this section 1, it should be an itinerant court travelling over the country. Who is asking for it? I do not think the people believe in it.
I think we should start paying increased salaries to some of the judges who earn their money by going out on circuit trying these cases to which I referred, at great personal sacrifice, having to live at country hotels and all that kind of thing, whereas these other judges can live here in the city of Ottawa.
As I say, we seem to think of Washington, not only politically, economically, financially and in military considerations, but we seem now to want to copy the United States in this matter. In everything we do here the first people we consider are the people of the United States. Now it is the judiciary. There is a difference between the court constituted by section 1 and the court in the United States. The court in the United States does not represent provinces or localities. Why should one province have four representatives? Why should we have that provision, if we are anxious to copy that system, as we are by section 1 of the bill? In the United States they do not have that principle at all. It is the principle that I am objecting to. I see little principle in the bill. If there were any principle in it, it would be another matter. But there is no principle in the bill except political considerations first, last and all the time. I can tell hon. members that there is a large body of lawyers who do not approve the principle that this court, if it is to be the Supreme Court of Canada, should represent localities. In the United States the best lawyers are chosen. One or two of them belong to New York state. I think New York state probably would get only one under this system. The best men at the bar are chosen there. The best men at the bar are plenty good enough for the Supreme Court of the United States.
The bar association did not believe in this proposal. The people back home in the constituencies do not believe in it. I fail to see any of the provinces asking for it. It is a huge waste of money. It is a waste of public funds which we and this government have no right to expend in this way; the government has no mandate from the people back home in the constituencies to go about it in this way. We can find other uses for our money than squandering it in this way. There is little principle in this bill except a political
Supreme Court Act
principle. That seems to be the sole consideration here.

Mr. Chairman, I hasten to express my opposition to the amendment, for it is inconsistent and offers no solution whatever to the problem now under consideration.
In fact the bill is nothing more than another measure of centralization on the part of the government.
In discussing the principle of the bill hon. members on the government side sought to avoid the issue by limiting their remarks to the abolition of appeals to the privy council, knowing full well that everyone is in favour of such a measure. In my opinion the practice of appealing to the privy council should have been abolished a long time ago.
The point on which we, of the opposition, disagree with the government is in maintaining that this bill should never be adopted in this house without first consulting the provinces.
The house is called upon to establish a final court to settle disputes which may arise between the central power and the provinces.
We find it inconsistent that only one of the parties to a pact should be called, or rather that it should arrogate to itself the right to determine alone what tribunal will decide on its disputes with the other party.
At the time of confederation, my province, and for that matter the other provinces as well, rejected the principle of a legislative union and agreed to become part of a federal state in which her rights and prerogatives would be protected.
The reason why the representatives of lower Canada, which is now the province of Quebec, consented to join the other provinces in forming the confederation was that they sincerely believed that, in the constitutional act implementing that pact, the language, religion, rights and traditions of the French minority in this country would be guaranteed and unequivocally recognized for the future.
That is why we opposition members now demand for the provinces a safeguard similar to that which the fathers of confederation had guaranteed to them.
But each day some fresh government pressure endangers the very spirit of the confederation pact.
This bill which, upon the whole, is an amendment to the constitution, and which is related to the other unilateral amendments promised in the speech from the throne, is a breach of the rights of provinces, if the latter are not consulted.
I am pleased to see that at least one Liberal member has felt remorse and, by means of an amendment, now endeavours to give the

Supreme Court Act
provinces an apparent advantage. But he does not understand what we claim for the provinces. It is not charity, but simply an acknowledgment of their rights.
On behalf of the provinces we cannot agree to the proposed amendment. It would be encroaching on their autonomy. It is up to the provinces to decide their fate for themselves, and the federal parliament must not force its will upon them.
As a citizen of the province of Quebec and as a French Canadian, it is my duty to vote against the amendment as presented.

speechtext:
Before clause 1 carries I should like to ask the minister this question. Has he given consideration to leaving the court at seven for the time being until we know just how much business there is to be handled and whether or not it is wise to increase the number to nine? It does seem to me that increasing it to nine in this way may bring up a good deal of trouble. There is the provision that three of the judges must come from Quebec. I imagine that Ontario will demand that at least three of the judges must come from that province, and that leaves three others. The four western provinces combined have practically the same population as Quebec, but a little smaller than Ontario. These provinces have different types of problems. Certainly British Columbia has problems quite different from those of the three prairie provinces. At the present time Alberta has problems arising which are quite a bit different from the problems of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The three western provinces have a claim to three judges on the supreme court if Ontario and Quebec are to have three. That would leave none at all for the three maritime provinces and for Newfoundland. In the case of Newfoundland there will be many new legal problems to be solved. I think that Newfoundland should have a judge on this supreme court and certainly Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island should have at least one and possibly two. If consideration is to be given to having a set number of judges from any one part of the country it hardly seems fair to me that eight provinces in the dominion should have only three judges on this court while the two great central provinces have three apiece.
As the government knows, there is a great deal of feeling abroad in the country that Ontario and Quebec outweigh the other provinces. There is a great deal of resentment against the fact that the two great provinces have more power in the nation than the more distant ones. That is quite a

serious difficulty. Has the minister given consideration to leaving the court at seven for the time being until we find some way to work out this question of the proper allocation? Under the law as it stands now Quebec is entitled to two judges and in practice I believe Ontario has also two judges. The west has two and the maritimes have one. Further consideration should be given to this particular proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend I might say that before drafting clause 1 of the bill in the form in which it now appears serious consideration was given to all of the factors to which my hon. friend has referred in the remarks he has just made.
So far as the reference in the clause to there being three appointees from Quebec is concerned, the necessity for that arises, as my hon. friend knows, from the fact that in that province they have a system of civil law which is altogether different in character from the common law that we inherited from England, and which prevails in the other provinces. While the clause says that the third judge shall be appointed from Quebec, the real purpose of making that appointment is to get upon the supreme court, when it becomes the court of last resort for Canadian lawsuits, three lawyers trained in the civil code rather than in the common law. It is that consideration, more than any geographical consideration of appointing a judge to represent this province or that one, that weighed in our deciding upon that particular subsection.
I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will agree that the arguments which he advanced with regard to the difficulties of securing representation upon the membership of the supreme court from each of the provinces of Canada would be somewhat-

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
No; but to secure geographical representation in the terms which the hon. member was stating would be obviously somewhat more difficult with seven members on the supreme court than it would be with nine. However, I am not for one moment suggesting that that consideration was a dominant factor in our thoughts in arriving at the idea that we should increase the membership from seven to nine members. We knew that when we created the supreme court as the court of last resort for Canada we would have to have appointed to the membership of that court enough civilians or judges trained in the civil law so that, in the event of there coming from Quebec a case involving any matters other than criminal law, it would be decided without a stalemate, having one civilian judge on one side and one

civilian judge on the other. That necessitated the appointment of three judges trained in the civil law on that court of last resort.
Then we thought

and I admit that in this we had to engage in some measure of surmise-that having regard to the volume of business which heretofore had come to the court, and having regard to the best estimate we could form as to what might come to it as the court of last resort in Canada, the actual amount of business to be transacted would necessitate an increase in the membership of the court.
In that connection my deputy consulted with the members of the court, and section 1 of the bill represents the best judgment of the department. This was recommended to the government and has been accepted, and we now recommend it to the House of Commons. Having regard to all the circumstances which apply, we believe it is wise that we increase the membership of the court to nine members, and that we should not delay or experiment with seven. It is our view that this increase should be made as soon as convenient after the passing of the bill.

speechtext: If this is to be a national federal court, why should we have the principle of representing localities? In Great Britain that principle is not followed; with their 47,000,000 people they do not have provinces. Why should not this court be a federal court, and not represent localities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I would not want anything I have said today to leave the impression that we regard it as a federal court representing localities. The intention is that we shall endeavour to get men of the very best legal ability in Canada to sit on this court, having regard to the fact that when it becomes a court of last resort for this country it will be exercising a type of jurisdiction considerably different from and much more onerous than that which it has exercised heretofore, when it was merely a court through which appeals went on their way to the court of last resort, the judicial committee of the privy council.
This being so, I believe there is a good deal of merit in the suggestion of the hon. member that it should be a federal court, and that the chief object should be to secure the very best talent available. Of course, if we can achieve that object and at the same time give representation to as many parts of Canada as possible, I am sure the hon. member would agree with me that the second objective is a desirable one so long as it can be attained without sacrificing the first.
So far as representation of Quebec is concerned, as I have already indicated, it is not in any sense a geographical representation, but rather one necessitated by the fact that, unlike other countries, we have in one of our larger and more thickly populated provinces a civil code, which is a system of law quite distinct from the common law. In making the Supreme Court of Canada the court of last resort we have to make adequate provision to hear appeals from all parts of Canada, including Quebec.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is one point concerning which I should like to be clear. I think the Minister of Justice has given the proper explanation why in a court of nine because of the difference in the civil law there should be three judges from the province of Quebec. However, there is another point about which I should like some explanation and that is why the words "at least" after the word "three" are inserted? The section is to read:
Three at least of the judges shall be appointed from among the judges of the Court of King's Bench, or of the Superior Court, or the barristers or advocates of the province of Quebec.
Why the words "at least"? The insertion of the words "at least" leaves it open to the appointment of four, five, or more from the province of Quebec. I remember the Prime Minister saying he thought that, rather than rely on statutory provisions and so on, the good will and good faith of the people across Canada was the best guarantee of justice for all. I am entirely of that opinion.
But I think the placing of the words "at least" in this section may give rise to controversy. I think it was ill advised to put

them there. They do not do anything at all, but they do leave the way open for argument that four, five, six, seven, eight or the whole court may be appointed from one province. Perhaps the Minister of Justice will explain that.
If this court is enlarged it should be representative of all Canada. It is true that there should be judges who understand the civil law of the province of Quebec, but beyond that it should be a court which represents all Canada. I think it would be wrong to infer that, because there are to be three appointed from the province of Quebec to deal with cases coming under their civil law, there must be three appointed from Ontario or three appointed from the mari-times or three appointed from western Canada or from any other section of the country. What I think the government should do in appointing judges to the supreme court is to choose those in the legal profession who are best qualified regardless of their geographical location in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar confirm what was said by the hon. member for Broadview, that it is desirable that in appointing members to this court first regard should be had to their capacity to discharge their judicial duties. If we can have geographical representation consistent with that policy of appointment, so much the better, but we should lay the greatest emphasis upon the capacity of the court.
I think the answer to my hon. friend's question would be in line with that concept. I am sure he will agree that in order to make a proper disposition of the cases from Quebec we cannot have less than three representatives from that province.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: I agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
If we said three, period, or three without adding the words "at least", that would indicate a geographical representation in a sense. In that way we could not, where the ability of a particular man was an issue, add to that number. There is in the history of the supreme court one example of that sort of thing. At one time when the "two" limitation was in force it was desired to appoint to the supreme court a man who, I think all hon. members will agree, would have been a great ornament to that court. He was a man who on one occasion was selected as sole arbitrator to settle a dispute between two South American countries. It was left to him solely to decide whether the dispute should be settled and on what terms.

This man had world renown as a lawyer both in common and in civil law. I refer to the late Eugene Lafleur. On that occasion when we might have had one of the finest legal minds that ever existed in Canada on the court, the government would have been unable to appoint him. It is true that Mr. Lafleur refused because he felt that he was getting on in years and could not stand the heavy duties involved in the highest type of judicial work.
I do not want the impression to be left from what I have said that it is a settled policy, that the government will invoke this power to appoint more than three judges from Quebec. It simply means that if some time later an extraordinary case such as that of Mr. Lafleur should arise, when there is a man the best qualified in Canada to fill a vacant appointment, he could be appointed if he should happen to live in Quebec.

speechtext: Where do we go from here if we pass this section? Where does Canada go if we pass section 1?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL

I am sure that this question must have arisen in the past and it must have been in the minds of the minister and his officials when this bill was being drafted. Could the minister tell us the considerations involved and whether it would be possible? It certainly would be most advantageous.

on circuit and properly dispose of the cases coming before it without holding up judgments.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: If hon. members will look at clause 2 on page 1 of the bill, following that to the bottom of the page and over to page 2 and to the bottom of that page, they will see there enacted new sections 36 to 40 inclusive, all of which are in clarification of the existing law, without any significant change in substance. Then going over to page 3 they will see a new section 41; and if they will look at the explanatory note opposite page 3 they will find a statement which I believe is quite exhaustive and which will enable my hon. friend to grasp the nature of this increase in jurisdiction authorized by new section 41. Section 41 is new, and in a sense is consequential in that it is an attempt-and I think a successful attempt-to provide in the Supreme Court of Canada the counterpart of that appeal jurisdiction which was exercised by the privy council upon special leave in respect of certain classes of cases that formerly went before it. So this new section 41 provides a considerable increase in the jurisdiction of the supreme court, as a court of last resort, to hear, upon leave, the type of cases referred to in the new section 41.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: As I understand it, there is no enlargement of the jurisdiction of the court to hear appeals, with respect to the financial amount involved? As I recall it there is a limit of $2,000, and that stands?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes. When the privy council was the court of last resort for Canadian appeals, there was a class-or classes-of

Supreme Court Act
appeals which could not be taken to the Supreme Court of Canada but which could be taken to the privy council. If we were to abolish appeals to the privy council without making provision for those classes of appeals formerly taken there, those appellants would be without a remedy by way of appeal. So the new section 41 provides in such cases an appeal upon leave to the Supreme Court of Canada, to replace that appeal they formerly had to the privy council, by leave.

speechtext: What section are we on, Mr. Chairman?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton will appreciate that in making this great jurisdictional change in the supreme court we intend to exercise extreme care with respect to the two additional appointments. There is that consideration and also the matter of consulting with the chief justice and the members of the court as to when they feel they can adequately carry on their new jurisdiction. subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
We are on the title, and the title is a misnomer, as no one knows better than this government. The proposed title of the bill is "An act to amend the Supreme Court Act," but no one knows better than the government that this is not a federal court in any sense at all. By this legislation the government is seeking to abolish statutory appeals, as well as appeals by grace, which has always been the inalienable right of every British subject.
If we adopt this bill, I ask the government: where do you propose to go from here? That is a simple question for them to answer. When we adopt the title of this bill the whole bill automatically goes through this house and receives the approval of parliament. Where does the government propose to go from here? Does it propose to stay in or get out of the British empire? That is exactly the question, especially when you consider

the various other steps that have been proposed. This is nothing but a political bill first, last and all the time; and I can tell you that it is going to lead to untold litigation, in view of the fact that we have reserved the right of appeals that have been undertaken up to the present time. This is weakening the ties to which I referred the other day, together with all these other motions with respect to the governor general, the flag, the anthem and so on. Why don't we get out of the empire, if we are going to pass a bill like this?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I want to discuss this bill on third reading. The principle of the bill and what it proposes to do are entirely different. Here we are going to abolish statutory appeals from the provinces, and I want to have a fair discussion of this bill, not under rules that are three hundred years old. This legislation affects every citizen of this country. We have to go away back to follow the history of it. Confederation was brought about by a contract between the provinces which formed the dominion, as no one knows better than the government. The other day I referred to the Statute of Westminster, on which the bill is founded, and the textbook in which it is stated that we have not the right to do what we are proposing today.
I want to make only a few remarks on the motion for third reading. I do not wish to object to it any further. I have alpiost exhausted my time. I think we should obey the Speaker and follow the rules of the house. I have never infringed upon the rules of the house and I do not propose to do so now. I point out to the government that there is a large body of informed public opinion in this country that is opposed to this bill. The four ministers of justice to whom I referred the other day as well as former chief justices of the Supreme Court of Canada were opposed to this policy. The Supreme Court Act was passed in 1875.
We are now violating all those pacts which the provinces had and to which reference

was made in the textbook by Wheare on the Statute of Westminster. This proposal would upset all that.
Mr. Howard Ferguson, when he was premier of Ontario, and the late Lord Bennett, when he was the leader of the House of Commons, opposed this policy. What is the reason for rushing this bill now? Certain statements were made during the election and while I wish to speak with respect of everyone in this house, I can tell you that in my opinion this is nothing but a political bill, first, last and always. Accordingly, it is put on the order paper ahead of many other motions. There is no doubt about that.

This is a rather important point of procedure. If there is any reason for delaying third reading, I certainly do not want to insist upon it. The government would be glad to consider any such reason. I think it would be rather interesting to
Supreme Court Act
have a ruling on the meaning of these standing orders 73 and 77. I had always understood that, when a bill received second reading and went into committee on the same day, and was reported out of committee on that day, it could not be read a third time without unanimous consent.

As it is in this case.

(putting the change if any)).
It is submitted that in view of that standing order, 77, and the rule, 810, there is no question but that the procedure we are following is the proper one.

810: "When shall the report be received?" The answer was "Now." I then asked the house, "When shall this bill be read a third time?" I received the answer "Now."
Standing order 73, which has been quoted by hon. members, reads as follows:
Every bill shall receive three several readings on different days, previously to being passed.
This bill had received two separate readings previously to today. The rule goes on to read as follows:
On urgent or extraordinary occasions, a bill may be read twice or thrice, or advanced two or more stages in one day.
With that rule must be read standing order 77, which is as follows:
All amendments made in committee are reported by the chairman to the house, which shall receive the same forthwith. After report the bill is open to debate and amendment, before it is ordered for a third reading. But when a bill is reported without amendment, it is forthwith ordered to be read a third time at such time as may be appointed by the house.
I would refer hon. members to the words "forthwith" and the references in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, which have been mentioned in debate by a number of members and also to the latter part of reference 705, Beauchesne's third edition. I shall not read these references but when they are considered along with standing orders 73 and 77, I think it is clear that it is in order for a bill to be read a third time on the same day that it is reported from the committee, provided that it has been reported without amendment.
I therefore rule that it is in order for this bill to be read a third time now.
