subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
All right, then. I sent my papers to the office. Under the rules of the house I am within my rights in saying something on this bill for twenty-five minutes in order to give hon. members a chance to come back. I cannot understand the necessity for this bill in view of the matters which I enumerated the other day as being primary. There are certain other matters which I referred to the other day which are secondary. The matters to which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred the other day are secondary. They are interwoven with different matters that have been placed on the order paper and were discussed during the election. What mandate have I, representing a constituency, to agree to this legislation? It was not discussed during the election.
I never heard of its being discussed in the Toronto district. The Prime Minister visited 
our city. He got a very great reception, and I was very pleased to see it. In no part of the country did he get a better reception. That was owing to the fact that he had been a great lawyer, a great family man and a great citizen, and had done a great deal for the people of this country as a private citizen long before he came to this house.
I now wish to say one or two things about certain matters that have come up in the debate. I never could understand the rush regarding this bill when one considers the other urgent matters which are before us. This matter is only secondary. I named the secondary matters the other day. I do not wish to name them again or to refer to any textbook. The intention seems to be to rush this particular proposal quickly through the house. That is the whole idea behind it. Why the necessity for that action? We might be a little more sportsmanlike in this house, and let the people who are not here return to deal with it. We might postpone it for at least twenty-four hours to give them a chance to come here.
With regard to the bill itself may I say, as I said the other day, I can find very little legal principle in it. The principle of the bill seems to be coercion. It is very largely a coercion bill because it is not founded on the pact made at confederation. You are going to change the whole legal system of this country in the twinkling of an eye without consulting anybody. For that reason I proposed that for bills of this description we should have a legal committee to which they could be referred. Nobody ever heard of this bill back in the constituencies. Today I received two letters from two high court judges out on circuit. They wanted to know whether I could send them a copy of the bill and of the debate that had taken place so far.
I did so this morning. They are out on circuit and they are trying important cases in various parts of the country. I have no way of letting them know without communicating with them.
Then there is the Canadian Bar Association. They had a meeting out in Calgary. They asked to have this legislation postponed. I cannot see the necessity for all the rush in connection with this bill. I cannot see the necessity for it apart from the basic fact that there are a lot of other proposals on the order paper. Under the rule of anticipation I cannot refer to them now and I do not intend to, but they are only secondary as well. We have grave questions facing us. We may be invaded. We do not know who is to come here in the next few days if we are to believe the reports which we get from Washington

and from Britain about the present danger in the Pacific, our back door. We do not know whether we are to be here very long.
I wish to call hon. members' attention to some important matters which should be dealt with at the present time. The matter to which we are now giving attention and such matters as the governor general, the flag, the anthem and the hallelujah chorus, are all secondary matters. We have had a hallelujah chorus on this bill. All these things could very well wait over. We have had nothing but hallelujah in here ever since the session opened. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have been singing the hallelujah chorus. If they went out and hired a concert hall they could make their fortunes as musicians.
In the first place I fail to see the urgency of this bill. What is the need for all the rush? The bar association expressed themselves at Calgary. I hold their resolution in my hand. Members of the bar of all Canada took part in that meeting. Nobody is a better lawyer than my friend the Speaker of the House of Commons. He has been a leading lawyer and soldier, and a good citizen, and all hon. members have been unanimous in expressing their pleasure at his being here.
The resolution adopted at the convention of the Canadian Bar Association dealing with the abolition of appeals to the privy council states:
Whereas the government of Canada has announced its intention to introduce legislation at the next session of the parliament of Canada, providing for the abolition of appeals to the privy council and making the Supreme Court of Canada our final court of appeal in all matters.
Be it resolved-
And here is the resolution:
-that the Canadian Bar Association, without expressing any view as to the wisdom or otherwise of the proposed abolition, is of the opinion:
(i) That any bill for the abolition of the privy council appeal should contain the necessary provisions as to the organization and jurisdiction of the supreme court and the system by which its judges will be appointed.
That sufficient time be given before the statute is enacted to permit the public-
"The public"?-they have never had one minute's consideration. I have never heard this discussed in the Toronto district by a single person, in the municipal, provincial or federal sphere. I doubt if there is a member from the Toronto district who has discussed this bill with his constituents. Yet we are asked to accept it today, holus-bolus, without knowing what it is all about. The resolution states:
That sufficient time be given before the statute is enacted to permit the public to give consideration, both as to the question whether the abolition of the appeal to the privy council should take place and to
Supreme Court Act
the constitution and powers of the court that may replace it and also to the effect which the abolition may have upon provincial and minority rights.
That is correct. And then it continues:
(ii) If, as and when the appeal should be abolished, it is the opinion of this association as at present advised:
(a)	that the supreme court should consist of nine judges;
(b)	that a quorum of the court should be five judges;
(c)	that it should sit always with an odd number of judges present:
They are going to be an odd lot, if we adopt this bill. And we will be an odd lot of members of the House of Commons if we swallow it holus-bolus. It continues:
(d)	that there should be no change in the present practice of the court, under which each member is free to give reasons for his judgment;
That may be all right. With many people, "I agree" is a popular phrase. "We agree" would be an unpopular phrase if we, in the high court of parliament, were to sit here and do nothing about this bill. To swallow it is just a loss of time. We are supposed to be the highest court in the land, but very often this is the forgotten branch of the legislature. Then the resolution continues:
(e)	that the court should continue to sit at Ottawa only;
I do not agree with that paragraph. The judicial committee of the privy council sits in London only because that is the centre of the empire. As a matter of actual fact, it could hardly be classified as a court, because they do not wear gowns, and they meet in an ordinary room. I know there are many people who would not agree to the proposed court sitting always in Ottawa. We realize of course that the judicial committee sits in London because that is the central point between east and west, and stands as one of the reasons why the court is not itinerant. It could well come to Ottawa, or go to Australia, New Zealand or South Africa if it so chose. The resolution continues:
(f)	that the salaries of the judges of the court should be substantially increased so as to make such salaries commensurate with the responsibilities of the office, with an appropriate additional amount to the chief justice;
I see no reason why we should spend as much money on eleven million people as is spent at Washington for one hundred and thirty million people. I have criticized that practice before, and have pointed out that too often we follow the United States.
I do believe however that the salaries of some of the judges in the trial courts throughout the province might very well be increased, particularly when they are doing circuit work. A man cannot afford to have a house, but most of them are keeping their homes. I believe there was a rule at one time-and

Supreme Court Act
Mr. Speaker may know more about this than I do-whereby judges of the court of appeal had to be residents of Toronto. I understand one of the great judges who came from the native city of Mr. Speaker proposed remaining in his own home town. It is very difficult to get housing accommodation in Toronto now; and that which is available costs about three times what it is worth.
I believe that the judges at Osgoode Hall have to have their homes in Toronto, and that it has been difficult for some of the new judges to get accommodation-even at three times the price. For five or six months of the year the trial judges are out on circuit throughout the province. They cannot be home with their wives and families for weeks on end. We have twelve judges in the trial division, and some of them are very tired of the accommodation they are able to get in hotels, and all that kind of thing. We should make provision for them accordingly.
Then, the next paragraph states:
(g)	that the rule of stare decisis ought to continue to be applied with respect to past decisions of the court, as well as with respect to past decisions of the judicial committee.
This is a rule of doctrine. An opinion was expressed not long ago by a prominent lawyer in Toronto, who quoted an Oxford professor who used these words:
No nation conscious of its own greatness and realizing of what national greatness consists can afford to do without the highly cultured citizen who is a vital power in civic and state affairs or the trained scholar whose function it is to keep up the quality and standard of culture.
And this lawyer goes on to say:
If the judicial committee of the privy council is no longer to be one of our courts of appeal the doctrine of stare decisis should be retained and its judgments remain precedents for all time.
That is what this Oxford professor has to say, and I believe there is much to be said for that principle. So far as possible, as a high court of parliament we should base our decisions on that doctrine. Let me say this about the bill which is now before us for third reading. I have before me a textbook. Hon. members are aware that the recent decision of the privy council is based on the Statute of Westminster. That is where this bill had its beginning; it started with the Statute of Westminster. This book is entitled "The Statute of Westminster and Dominion Status". For 99 pages it deals with the dominion status in 1926. In that section it deals with Ontario and Quebec, the two original provinces, and reference is made to the maritimes and the status of the dominion generally. It then goes on to refer to the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Australia and other parts of the British

empire. It calls attention to the fact that the process of appeals to the privy council was based upon a contract.
When Mr. Ferguson was premier of Ontario he objected to the suggestion that appeals to the privy council be abolished and he directed attention to the debates on this matter which had taken place since confederation. He said that there was no doubt that a contract had been made by the two original provinces and the same principle had been applied to the maritimes where objections had been raised during the war to the legal status. He went on to say that the procedure of amending the constitution should be accepted by the province of Ontario.
Ontario was against abolishing appeals to the privy council and they prepared a brief which was placed before the cabinet here in Ottawa. That brief was addressed to a very learned attorney general who was minister of justice. I referred to three or four of them the other day. The Prime Minister was about to leave to attend an imperial conference and this brief was presented in connection with abolishing appeals to the privy council. Mr. Howard Ferguson prepared this brief while he was premier of Ontario. That brief states:
-that no restatement of the procedure for amending the constitution of Canada can be accepted by the province of Ontario that does not fully and frankly acknowledge the right of all the provinces to be consulted and to become parties to the decision arrived at. Quebec and all the other provinces proved to be in agreement with these views. In consequence it was necessary for the Canadian delegation at the imperial conference of 1930 to ask that, in effect, the whole question of the repeal of the Colonial Laws Validity Act, in its application to Canada, should be left in suspense until the views of the provinces on the matter could be obtained.
Mr. Ferguson was quite correct and the reference to the Dominion of Canada and to the provinces of Canada was therefore deleted from the proposed clause, as it appeared in the schedule drawn up by the conference with a specific reference to Australia and New Zealand only. It was stated that a section dealing exclusively with the Canadian position would be inserted after the representations of the provinces had received consideration. At the same time the conference deemed it advisable to place on record that the sections of the statute relating to the Colonial Laws Validity Act should be so drafted as not to extend to Canada unless the statute was enacted in response to such requests as are appropriate to an amendment of the British North America Act. It was also deemed desirable to place on record the view that the sections should not subsequently be extended to Canada except by an act of the parliament of the United Kingdom enacted in response

to such requests as are appropriate to an amendment of the British North America Act.
The conference of federal and provincial governments was held in Canada in April 1931, to consider this whole question of appeals to the privy council and of consulting the provinces thereon. The late Lord Bennett was then Prime Minister of the dominion. All the provinces were present at that conference which was held here in Ottawa, including the great provinces of Quebec and Ontario.
As it is six o'clock I should like to move the adjournment of the debate until tomorrow at three o'clock.

subtopic: CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is similar to one I introduced last session but which, owing to the dissolution of the 20th parliament it did not come up for second reading. This bill differs in one respect, in that it merely requires the permanent installations of the railway companies to comply with local smoke abatement by-laws. I have amended the bill in this regard following some conversations I had with railway officials when the bill was in a rather more specific form. From time to time both railway companies have said to me that to impose upon them some specific apparatus or some specific smoke abatement regulations would be unfair when industries, ships and other smoke producers are permitted to pollute the air without abatement. Therefore this bill would add paragraph (1) to section 287 of the Railway Act, as follows:
(1) requiring ail roundhouses and other permanent installations to comply with any municipal bylaw of any urban municipality regulating the emission of smoke or soot into the atmosphere but such orders and regulations shall not apply to locomotives in motion;
Railway Act
So in this amendment we merely seek to abate the nuisance of smoke produced by railway roundhouses. The problem to be solved is this. Coal-burning locomotives have to be serviced regularly. This servicing requires that steam pressure be maintained in the boilers; and when major repairs are to be made and the fire is drawn, consequently the fire has to be relit. These operations result in inefficient combustion of the fuel, which in turn produces smoke, soot or smog. I want to point out that the production of smoke now is a sign of inefficiency. In the old days we would say that smoking chimneys were the sign of a hardworking, industrial community. Today a smoking chimney is a sign of waste. But owing to the requirements in connection with fueling and servicing locomotives this problem does arise and, with the exception of some cases where special apparatus has been installed, these roundhouses do emit smoke or smog into the atmosphere, which unquestionably is a serious discomfort to those living in the vicinity.
Now we come to the responsibility of the various authorities concerned. It would be unfair to ask a railway company to make a roundhouse comply with certain regulations, unless in order to protect the residents the municipality had enacted an enforceable antismoke bylaw. So in order to prevent discrimination against the railway companies I have drawn the bill so that it merely asks roundhouses to comply with the regulations which have been worked out for smoke abatement and which apply to all other industries in the district.
The specific instance with which I wish to deal is the roundhouse in my own constituency, the main roundhouse of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in what are known as the Lambton yards, where nearly all the locomotives are serviced for that company in the Toronto area. There are other roundhouses in downtown Toronto, but the one in the Lambton yards is located in an area containing other industries, all of which have installed smoke abatement equipment, so they are not a real menace to the residents of that community. The only menace is this railway roundhouse. It may interest hon. members to learn that the precipitation in tons of soot per acre per year is said to be greater there than in any other city in Canada or the United States, with two exceptions. As a matter of fact a great part of central York township is more intensely sullied by smoke than any other area on this continent. It is infinitely worse than the city of Pittsburgh where a great deal of this remedial machinery has been installed. So we come to the inevitable conclusion that it is not necessary

Railway Act
for a roundhouse to emit smoke in such great quantities, as is the case in the Lambton yards.
There are several roundhouses in this metropolitan area. One roundhouse in the city of Toronto has installed what is known as a steam-generating plant. The locomotives enter this roundhouse and are serviced by means of this permanent steam-generating plant which has a smoke abatement apparatus installed on it. This roundhouse is not a menace to the residents situated near it. When I introduced this bill, it was suggested that the cost of installing such a system would not be worth while. That is merely an opinion, Mr. Speaker. I have not received adequate data to support that statement, nor have I received adequate data to support the suggestion that this steam plant would cost approximately $200,000.
We come to the next point, and that is that the railway companies are converting to diesel locomotives, certainly for switching purposes. In Toronto, I believe the switching locomotives are now almost completely dieselized. This is an improvement but, at the same time, the main line locomotives still burn coal. It is these main line locomotives which cause most of the smoke and soot in the area of which I complain.
Leaving my own constituency and turning to Ottawa, I might say that the other day I noticed a report in the press concerning the enforcement of the Ottawa municipal smoke bylaw. It was stated prosecutions would be launched unless the users of coal-burning equipment complied with the regulations. Unless some amendment such as this is written into the Railway Act, that would mean that other users of coal in Ottawa would be proscribed by the municipal regulations but the roundhouse in Ottawa west would be permitted to emit as much smoke as it desired.
At this point I should like to mention the regulations concerning the emission of smoke by roundhouses. Those regulations require that roundhouses may emit smoke of no greater density than Ringleman's density chart No. 3 for a period of ten minutes per hour. Reading Ringleman's density chart, Mr. Speaker, is something akin to a Philadelphia lawyer deciding what is hard and what is soft. It is a card with a hole in it through which one looks, and around the edges of which are varying degrees of black. I doubt very much whether any two people, or a court of law for that matter, could agree upon what was density 3, density 2 or density 4. Density 5 is almost completely opaque.
I believe that these regulations were written about 1908. In my opinion, they are obsolete. Modern technological progress in

smoke abatement requires that something new and better be worked out to protect residents near roundhouses.
It has been suggested that municipal enforcement officers should judge the smoke emitted by the roundhouses in the same manner as they judge the smoke emitted from an industrial plant. Any appeal would be to the board of transport commissioners, as in all other cases under the Railway Act. I had hoped, and I still hope, that the subject matter of this bill might be sent to the railway committee. A good deal of technical information, Mr. Speaker, must be brought forward before a solution to this problem can be found. It would only be fair to allow the railway committee to hear testimony from both sides concerning this matter. I also realize there are always some people who will complain no matter what progress is made.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. In the area of which I speak not only is it impossible to put out washing at any time on any day of the week, but even in the hottest weather windows must'be kept closed because of the constant seepage of soot under doors and windows, and through crevices. It makes living an intolerable burden to many of the people in that district. Furthermore, even a considerable distance from this roundhouse, if one digs down into the soil one finds a layer of soot and coal dust sometimes more than an inch thick. The houses are black and the whole life of the community is blighted by this smoke.
I am appealing to the house and to the government, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of these people. I am appealing to have this problem brought before a tribunal where those who oppose any improvement, as well as those who actually suffer from the present situation, can be heard.
This is something that affects the lives of many thousands of people in the city of Toronto and the county of York. It is a question to which there is a solution; it is a difficulty which can be and is being solved by the installation of steam-generating equipment and by other less costly means. It is a problem which can be solved if there is the willingness to solve it. On the one side of the equation there is the cost of putting in this smoke-abating equipment; on the other side of the equation is the life, health and comfort of thousands of individuals. I believe that I speak and plead the case for all those who have to put up with this everlasting smoke and soot which emanates from the roundhouse that I particularly complain of.

I represent a district which is probably suffering more

from smoke and soot than any other residential district in Canada. I refer to the lower section of ward 1, south of Queen street, in which lies the right of way of the C.N.R. over the Don river. It is a soldiers' district that I represent. There are a large number of homes there. During the heat wave the temperatures reached 95, 97 and 98 degrees Fahrenheit at night. Some of the soldiers are living in hovels not fit to live in. Because of the smoke, soot, oil and other things that escape from these engines the mothers must shut the windows at night.
In the first place, we have none of these diesel engines, as far as I can see, and I have looked out the window many times at the place where I live. They are shunting backwards and forwards through this district, assembling cars of all descriptions, making up trains and all that kind of thing. These soldiers' children suffer at night, during the heat. I remember that I received complaints from physicians in the district. They were complaining about the children getting throat trouble, asthma, and bronchitis, and that their lungs, when examined, are found to be filled with this material that escapes from these engines. Not only that, but boats on the route to St. Catharines, and others that put out from the east end of Toronto bay emit the same thing, with the result that the mothers are complaining to me. I am sorry that I have not the letters with me, so that I might read one or two of them.
I do not wish to speak for more than four or five minutes because I think that the hon. member who introduced the bill has covered the points well and deserves a great deal of credit for bringing the bill forward.
Hon. members will notice what the Railway Act provides. They will notice the amendments which have been made. They started long before I was in the house. The Railway Act is chapter 170 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. Amendments were made in 1928, 1929, 1930, 1932-33, 1938, 1946, 1947 and 1947-48. That is the general Railway Act. The board is now known as the board of transport commissioners; it used to be known as the board of railway commissioners. I may say that I have had some correspondence with the present board about this particular matter and about these soldiers' families, as well as with the housing authorities and others. Some of these families are living in the basement, below the ground, in hovels not fit for habitation. I have complained to the health department and to the city hall about it, but we can get no relief. What is to become of these children?
I have seen these children dragged off the street at night so that they might be put to bed, and when they go to bed they must 45781-431
Railway Act
endure these conditions; and the mothers are suffering intolerable conditions. The viaduct also passes through this district, and it is not a fit place of habitation for children. I am sorry that nothing is done for them. I am tired of making these complaints. I have made them right along ever since I have been a member representing the constituency of Broadview in the city of Toronto. I have complained before about this evil which exists.
Three physicians wrote me letters in which they complained about the throat trouble which they have encountered. These poor children have no place to play except in the street. Some of them have been knocked down by hit-and-run drivers. I know of a street-I think it is called Morse street; it is below Queen street-where the pavements were moved and so forth, and where little children have been knocked down and killed; but the authorities could not find who did it.

I ask hon. members to mark those words "of their own volition." They have engineers and officials, and many other people. I noticed in the House of Commons the other day we had an increase in the estimates for the board of transport commissioners. As I said the other day, we have a most able chairman now in Mr. Justice Archibald, but he has been too busy with the freight rate increases to give consideration to these matters. I hope that the government and particularly the minister responsible for housing and the health department will be able to do something in the matter. Nothing affects health more than this condition. Anyone who has come into Toronto from lake Ontario will I think agree that the smoke menace in that city is a serious one. From lake Ontario you can see the smoke of Toronto long before you can make out the shore line. But I believe there is a far worse menace with regard to smoke than railway roundhouses. The town in which I live, Brockville, is a large terminal of the Canadian National Railways and as such naturally we have

Railway Act
servicing of locomotives. There is naturally a certain amount of smoke that comes from the roundhouses and from the repair shops where those locomotives are being serviced. If one is on the river and looks towards the shore, one can see smoke coming up, but it is largely dissipated in the air. There are also in the town factories which emit a certain amount of smoke, although there is a town bylaw which keeps that condition fairly well under control. But we have a smoke menace far worse than the roundhouse; it is the uncontrolled smoke of lake steamers.
Anyone who lives along the waterways of the great lakes system will know what I mean. The smoke from one steamer is greater in volume than the smoke coming out of all the locomotives that are being serviced and from all the factories in Brockville. I say that without fear of contradiction, and anyone who has seen that will know that I know whereof I speak. It is a serious menace. It is detrimental to the housewife who has to put out her washing. Her whole morning's wash can be spoiled by one ship going by. The smoke seeps into the houses. The type of fuel these steamers burn must be the very lowest type of bituminous fuel. It infiltrates into everything, particularly when traffic is very heavy, as it was yesterday on the St. Lawrence. The whole atmosphere is permeated. It lies all along the shore line. You cannot see very far. I believe the modern terminology for it is smog, smudgy fog. I feel that steps must be taken by the railway committee to see that some solution is arrived at to stop this serious polluting of our atmosphere. We have pollution of water and we have pollution of atmosphere. I am firmly of the opinion that, of the two, pollution of the atmosphere is worse, because you can always filter and chlorinate the water; but the poor human beings are compelled to stand there and breathe the atmosphere. Doctors have told me that there are many serious detrimental gases and acids that we absorb through breathing this contaminated air.
The time has definitely arrived when something concrete must be brought before the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to enforce not only a cleaning up of smoke emanating from roundhouses but more particularly from the lake steamers which apparently do not wish to co-operate with the public in abolishing the smoke nuisance.

the situation with which the hon. member for York West dealt so adequately. I have lived in the part of Toronto known as West Toronto for many years. Only very recently, in fact not until after June 27, did anyone think it was worth while asking my opinion as to what should be done to alleviate the smoke nuisance, but I have a personal knowledge of it. As a matter of fact it is public knowledge in West York and in the High Park riding that the St. Clair-Runnymede section has for many years suffered from this particular condition. I believe the Canadian Pacific Railway roundhouse was built in 1912. When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) starts to take my speech apart I hope he will forgive me if I have made any misstatements of fact because it was only on Sunday afternoon that I got the information which I now intend to give to the house.
In 1912 a roundhouse was built at the corner of St. Clair avenue and Runnymede road. It has 33 smokestacks disseminating smoke in the neighbourhood, and it operates with an impartial hand. Smoke falls on the Liberals, Conservatives and C.C.F. impartially and alike. It is very bad. In that particular section as far back as 1912, sir, I well recall that no houses were built in that area because of the smoke hazard. That is quite evident from the way the neighbourhood developed. Up until after the first great war no one built much in the area. It was known as the Scarlet Plains. As boys we went there to play cops and robbers. Our mothers asked us to hurry home because after dark it was not considered safe. There was very little habitation there. South of the tracks that same condition persisted. No one bothered to build a house there. Anyone who owned property there just simply let it stand. If you will search the registry office in Toronto you will find that most of the titles there are tax deed titles. No one wanted it. The reason was the smoke which was disseminated over this entire area. It never affected me because fortunately I lived in a part of west Toronto which was far distant from the railroad. Occasionally when we would have a northeast wind I would hear my mother complaining about the fact that she had to take her washing in. There is a situation here which should be brought to the attention of this house.
After the first war there was a considerable development, and criticism of what the railroads were doing began to become vocal. After and during the second world war a great many houses were built. This is serviced land. I would assume that there are many thousands of people now living in that area, who have good homes, and who are

suffering from this menace. That the situation can be corrected is evident from the information which has been given to me. I understand that in the city of Toronto there are two other roundhouses: one known as the John street roundhouse and the other known as the Spadina avenue roundhouse. The John street roundhouse is operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There the engines are oil fired. Steam pressure is available so that the engines do not have to stay in the roundhouse until they are completely ready for service. They can go out under their own pressure to the water tank and then go about their business. In that way smoke is disseminated and does not become a hazard in only one localized area.
At the Spadina avenue roundhouse they have overcome the difficulty to an extent in this way. They have built one central smokestack and whenever an engine is being serviced the smoke from that particular engine is funnelled by fans into this one central smokestack and carried high up in the air and is given a chance to dissipate itself. I am informed that the Canadian Pacific Railway claim that they are doing everything within their power to alleviate the situation. They refer to the fact that they have diesel engines in Toronto and they are dieselizing their system. As I understand it, there are 19 diesel engines in Toronto, 10 of which operate out of the Lambton roundhouse. There are 80 coal-burning engines which are serviced from the Lambton roundhouse. These engines are disseminating their smoke over the entire area. If, Mr. Speaker, you had the time, the opportunity and the inclination to visit that district you would see, as the hon. member for York West has pointed out so strikingly, smoke-blackened houses. They have built up an entire new area there, and I wish to support most strongly the demand which the hon. member for York West has made to have the situation alleviated. Whether it should be done by the particular method which he has suggested in his bill or whether it should be done by amendment to the Railway Act I do not know. I have not gone into that particularly, but I do suggest to the Minister of Transport that he give this his earnest consideration. There is a real problem to be solved. The city of Toronto, the township of York and the ratepayers associations of St. Clair avenue and Maybank have organized themselves over the years, and have acquired a great deal of information which the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) has given the house tonight.
These people are greatly concerned about the depreciation in value of their properties.

I do feel however I should commend him upon bringing forward this bill for a second time, and also those who have contributed to the discussion.

Railway Act
There can be no doubt that the emission of smoke from roundhouses is a matter of considerable anxiety to the railways and also to the board of transport commissioners. It is a great nuisance, I am sure, to those people who, as the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) has pointed out, live in concentrated centres. There is no doubt, too, that it is not always easy to find a remedy for a situation, be it as intolerable as the hon. member has described it, or as it has been described by several hon. members who have spoken.
I doubt whether the solution proposed by the hon. member is the right one. However, before dealing with that I believe the house should know something about what has been done and what is now being done by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and by the railways to do away with some of the difficulties which arise through smoke emission from roundhouses, and also because of the nuisance in general.
For at least a year the board of transport commissioners has been giving this problem careful and serious attention. In the first place they saw to it that full-time inspectors were appointed. These inspectors were charged with the responsibility of studying the smoke nuisance, interviewing employees, giving instructions, and suggesting how they might improve the situation in roundhouses and in handling locomotives generating steam. The reports of these employees come to the board from time to time; they are examined, and by reason of them some improvements are made by the railways.
The second step taken by the board of transport commissioners was to see to it that the railway companies installed special equipment on steam switching locomotives for the purpose of abating smoke. A recent check by the board discloses that all steam yard engines working in the Toronto territory have now been equipped with what are known as over-fire jets for the purpose of eliminating complaints in connection with smoke from locomotives.
Then, in the last few years the railways have been doing a tremendous job by way of diesel operations. I shall deal with the city of Toronto in a moment, but I think I should outline the situation generally. There are several kinds of diesel locomotives. First there is the diesel which operates the freight train which moves from one end of the country to the other. Then, there is the diesel locomotive which pulls the passenger train; and there is the diesel in which I should think at the moment the house is particularly interested, namely the one which does the switching. The more diesels the
[Mr. Chevrier.l
railways can purchase and employ on switching operations, the more can the nuisance from smoke and soot be abated.
Ten years ago there was practically no utilization of diesel engines. Five years ago the position was a little better. As I said a moment ago, in the last few years the railways have been doing an excellent job in the way of purchase of diesels. For instance, the number of diesel road locomotives at present in use in Canada totals 36. Six of these are operated by the Canadian National Railways, and 30 by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
The number of diesel switching locomotives at present in use in Canada stands at 172, and as I said a moment ago that is the class or kind in which the house is more interested at the moment.

(1) requiring all roundhouses and other permanent installations to comply with any municipal by-law of any urban municipality regulating the emission of smoke or soot into the atmosphere but such orders and regulations shall not apply to locomotives in motion:
I am informed that in order to install devices to completely eliminate smoke in the roundhouses of the larger centres only would cost a minimum of $24,000,000, and that is for the Canadian Pacific alone. I am informed also that to install these in other centres which would require them from time to time would cost about $42,000,000. Assuming the same cost for the Canadian National Railways, it would mean a total of $84,000,000. A diesel switcher costs $110,000, per unit, while a diesel road locomotive costs about $250,000 per unit. How many diesel switchers do hon. members think would be purchased if installations such as these had to be placed on the roundhouses, even in Toronto alone?
I wanted to deal with the legality of this bill. I do not think it is ultra vires, although I do feel it comes rather close to the line. However, I submit that it is bad legislation because it would tell the board of transport commissioners, who have jurisdiction in matters of this kind, that they must comply with the bylaws of municipalities. Supposing a municipality passed a bylaw providing that roundhouses should not emit smoke from five a.m. until eleven a.m. or possibly noon, the time during which railroads are busiest. There would be nothing in this bill to stop a municipality from acting in such a manner. If they did it would interfere with the efficient operation of the railroad and accordingly would not be a good thing for them.
While this legislation might not be ultra vires, I submit that it certainly is not good legislation. It is the type of legislation known as legislation by adoption. In other words, we would be setting up a board to do certain things and then putting a clamp on it by saying that it must not do other things unless a municipal corporation says thus and so.

I wish to continue for a few moments the remarks I was making when the house rose at six o'clock. In conclusion I should like to point out certain features about this legislation. The bill now before us for third reading is one of those matters which should be looked into further. I remember what the supporters of the bill have said, but in my opinion the proposals should be looked into further. I had my hand on some details a moment ago but I cannot find them.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) wants to rush this bill through for some reason best known to himself. The proposals which I refer to are set out in the bill. As I have said before, Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire. If she was going to be talked out of the British empire, she would have been talked out long ago. She will have to be fought out of the British empire.
I think we all remember what happened back in the thirties. Those were dark days for Canada, but the mother country came to our rescue with preferential treatment which brought about increased trade. If we adopt this proposal we are going to lose all that. We all know that Mr. Fielding once advised the adoption of preferences, and the six cent preference on wheat was adopted. There is no doubt that the Liberal party rounded it out and made a success of it. It all started away back in 1897 after Sir Wilfrid Laurier was prime minister. He gave the six cents per bushel on wheat. It took a long time to accomplish results and it was not until the thirties when there was a world depression that the prime minister of Great Britain and other prime ministers met here in Ottawa and adopted what were known as the Ottawa agreements. The man who was leader of the house then is now dead.
If you ask me, I think we are going a long way in this proposed bill. Why is it necessary to get it through tonight? Many government members are absent, together with members of other parties. Who is causing all

this upset; who is responsible for this jumpy style of doing business in the House of Commons, when we have the bar association, the provinces, the attorneys general and others asking that the matter be given further consideration? We need men in this house like the late Clarke Wallace, Dalton McCarthy, and the late John Ross Robertson and others who were here years ago, who would forget all about the party system and think only of the country first, last and all the time. We need men of that stamp in this House of Commons today.
As I was saying before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, we must go back a long way to get the history of this thing; but there will always be an England and there will always be an empire. This legislation is largely founded on the separatist doctrine, because that doctrine holds that the supreme court should be the ultimate court in Canada. In its issue of Monday, September 26, an important newspaper in Toronto had this to say:
Canada cannot at present amend her own constitution or settle her own law cases in her own courts. "Badges of colonialism," exclaims the Minister of Justice. Mr. Garson is right; and right, too, in saying that these badges should be "stripped off."
Then they go on to name someone who they think should be governor general. Half a dozen names have been suggested for that post. One is the chief justice of Canada; another is a former prime minister; another is Malcolm MacDonald. If you look at the proposed bill you will see that it is in two sections, one dealing with what might be called statutory appeals and the other with appeals of grace. Where are we going now under 20th century Liberalism if we are going to take away from a private citizen the right to petition the king? We must not forget that notwithstanding this legislation he is still the king of Canada, as he is the king of New Zealand and the king of Australia. He cannot divide himself in two; he is still and always will be the king of Canada.
We have had the Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, the Petition of Rights, and all the rest of those things. Every British subject, whether he lives in England, in Quebec, in Ontario, in the west, in New Zealand or Australia, has had the right to appeal to the foot of the throne with regard to his citizenship and also with regard to his property and civil rights and his liberty as a subject. Several distinguished men have occupied the position of minister of justice in this country. I have referred to Sir Allen Aylesworth, who was a brilliant lawyer; Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who was minister of justice, attorney general and solicitor general, lieutenant governor of Quebec and chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada; Sir Lomer Gouin, and

others. We have aiSO had many outstanding men as attorneys general of the provinces.
In dealing with what has brought about separatism I referred to a brilliant textbook on the Statute of Westminster, and how it affected New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and the other dominions and crown colonies.

Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian, as a Liberal, and as one who takes second place to no one in my loyalty to the British commonwealth, I strongly protest against the unjustifiable and unfounded claims being made that legislation of this type is in some way selling out Canada's interest in the commonwealth of nations. I would ask this house whether Canada, when it adopted its own Royal Canadian Navy, abandoned the British empire; whether Canada, when it adopted its own Royal Canadian Air Force, was abandoning the British empire; whether Canada, when it gradually learned to stand on its own feet, was abandoning the British empire. Or did we assist in maintaining the British empire and the British commonwealth of nations? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it is not a fact that because this country had learned to stand on its own feet and make its own decisions it has been able, during the recent war and since, by means of the Atlantic pact, to make a contribution not only to the British commonwealth but to the world at large of which Canada has no occasion to be ashamed. And I suggest that it is high time somebody expressed that view in this house.
With respect to this bill may I, as a new member who perhaps should not be raising his voice on this occasion at all, suggest that Canada had ample opportunity last June, and took advantage of that opportunity, to decide on the principle. I suggest also that this house has had ample opportunity during the past month, and particularly on the motion for second reading, to decide on the principle of the bill. maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON AS PRESIDENT OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
APPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON AS PRESIDENT OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) made an announcement of considerable importance. Briefly, I should like to make an observation or two about that announcement. In so far as that announcement contained news of the retirement of Mr. Vaughan from the presidency and chairmanship of the board of the Canadian National Railways, 1 think all members of the house would heartily join with the minister in the well-merited tribute he paid to that gentleman. However, the minister proceeded to announce the appointment of Mr. Donald Gordon to succeed Mr. Vaughan in the two offices of president and chairman of the board.
At the outset, I should like to make it quite clear that in thgse brief remarks I am speaking for myself, and I do not claim to speak for anyone else. Moreover, I do not wish anyone to construe anything I may say about the appointment as a personal reflection in any sense upon Mr. Donald Gordon. What I have to say concerns the principle at stake in the appointment. So far as Mr. Gordon is concerned, I respect him as a man of great ability, a man of vigour. I say, Mr. Speaker, that in the appointment which has been announced the government has done violence to an important principle, the principle that hard work and faithful service should be recognized within an organization by promotion.
These two positions are positions of great importance. I do not suppose there are half a dozen positions in the whole of this country that are more important than the positions which have been filled in the way indicated by the government today. As I said, the principle which in my submission has been violated is the principle that the office should be filled by promotion and that faithful service should be rewarded by promotion.
tMr. Church.]
It ought to have been possible to fill these high offices by promotion within the executive organization of the Canadian National Railways. Was that impossible, Mr. Speaker? I say this: If it was found to be impossible then it is a reflection upon the administration of that great institution. In a great organization of that kind, those charged with executive responsibility should be seized at all times with the responsibility of bringing on men capable of assuming greater executive responsibility. If, in the view of the government, such a man was not available within that organization then I say he should have been. If such a man was not available, then there has been some failure. Personally, I am disposed to believe that there were men of proven executive ability within the Canadian National Railways who are capable of meeting the demands of these two high offices.
I recall to you, sir, that when Mr. Hunger-ford was appointed president of the Canadian National Railways, that appointment was hailed by the government because it represented the appointment of a man who had worked his way up within the system. Similarly, when Mr. Vaughan was appointed president, the same thing was said, and rightly said. Here was the evidence for all to see. The reward of the highest rung on the ladder within the Canadian National Railways organization was available to those who were prepared to work and give faithful and devoted service.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON AS PRESIDENT OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
What do we find here? We find an appointment has been made which, in my view, is going to be very damaging to the morale of the organization. It simply means that those who have been carrying the responsibility in the organization are being told by the actions of this government that the top rung of the ladder is closed. It is not open to them. It will not be open for some time, in view of the fact that Mr. Gordon is, I believe, still in his forties. This means that those who have reached executive rank in that organization and those who, in the ordinary course, might expect to reach executive rank within the next few years, find that there has been a limit placed on the steps in the ladder that may be attained by promotion within the system.
It is the boast of the railways in the United States, and it is based upon ample evidence, that within the railway system there is a career open to merit. You will find that boast made throughout the railways of the United States, time after time, as one man comes to the presidency or a position of leading executive importance. In one railway

after another, you will find that the man has started on the lowest rung of the ladder in the railway system, whether as a section hand or train crew or any other position and has worked his way up until he has been rewarded with the highest executive position in the gift of the company-a career open to merit. And why should it not be so in Canada?
By the action of this government, those who had hoped there would be a career open to merit within the Canadian National Railways system, a career open right to the top, are now told that the career ends before the top rung of the ladder can be reached. That is one aspect of the principle, sir, involved in this appointment today. It is that principle to which violence has been done by the government.
The second aspect is that Mr. Gordon, with all his ability-and again I am stressing that I am not making any personal issue of this- is completely without experience in railroading. So far as I know, Mr. Gordon may not even have sought the office. I should like to tell the house, though, that a knowledge of railroading is not something that one can pick up in a month or two. I expect some hon. members of this house have had some experience in railroading. Over the past twenty years I have had considerable experience of a legal nature with railways, and I have had enough contact with them to know that the railway business is an exceedingly complicated one; it has many ramifications. The complexity of the business extends to its organization, its operations and to the manifold problems that railways face. A man without any experience at all in railroading has now been made chief executive officer of the Canadian National Railways.
The third aspect of the principle involved in this appointment is the question of how far the government is warranted in interfering with normal management and operation of a government-owned railway system. In my submission the Canadian National Railways system will function best if the government does not interfere with its management. If we are to have interference by government in the management of the railway, then the attempt of the Canadian National Railways to carry on efficiently will be bedevilled at every turn. I wish to pay this tribute to Mr. Vaughan. Throughout his tenure of office as president and chairman of the board, Mr. Vaughan sought to maintain that principle and to operate the system without interference of a political nature.
It is quite true that the statute under which this appointment has been made contemplates that the government should have
45781-44i

Canadian National Railways a voice in the appointment. Section 10, subsection 1, of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1936, which is chapter 25 of the statutes of that year, provides as follows:
The directors shall appoint, subject to the approval of the governor in council, a president of the national company who may be the chairman of the board of directors, or a person, other than one of the directors. The president, as such, shall hold office during the pleasure of the directors and, notwithstanding anything in this act, shall be paid by the national company such sum, salary or remuneration as the governor in council may approve.
It is clear that what the statute contemplates is that power of appointment should rest in the hands of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway Company, with a veto in the hands of the governor in council. It does not contemplate that the appointment of the president and chairman of the board should initiate with the government. With regard to the principle that I have submitted to the house as a desirable one to maintain, namely, that there should not be government interference in the operation of this railway system, I say to the house that great damage has been done today by the government. If this parliament really approves the principle of rewarding faithful service with promotion, then certainly we representing the people of Canada will wish to be an ideal employer as far as that may be possible. Representing the people of Canada as we do, we want to be the kind of employer who will be an example to other employers. In this government's action today, is there a worthy example to other employing organizations? I submit not. I submit that this is the kind of action that discourages people, when they see that the top jobs are not to be won by faithful service within the organization, when they see that these jobs go to people brought in from the outside by a government.
In my humble opinion there is far too much of this sort of thing throughout the government service generally, and it is going to be no help to the Canadian National Railways to see this sort of thing carried to the extent to which, in my submission, it is carried in the announcement made today, taking the plums and denying them to those who have worked faithfully within the service and who were legitimately entitled to feel that those plums were within their reach if they qualified within the fair rules of work. It is not simply a question of the effect on those who hold executive rank today; it is a question of the effect on the morale of every one right down to those on the lowest rung of the ladder in the whole Canadian National Railways system, when they see that this career is no longer one open to merit all the way through but is

Canadian National Railways open to merit only until they advance so far, and that the plums at the top are not to be won by faithful service.
Whatever may be said about the merits of Mr. Donald Gordon as a capable man-and again I emphasize the fact that I am making no reflection on him personally; I am not making a personal issue of this with regard to Mr. Gordon; I would have the same thing to say with regard to any appointment the government might have made today of anybody who had not been drawn from within the Canadian National Railways service-I think there is at stake here a vital principle that this house ought to vindicate, and that this principle has been shamefully violated in the government's decision that has been reported.

One argument used by my hon. friend was that the appointment of Mr. Donald Gordon would be unpopular with the men because he

did not belong to them. That was his argument. On that point he did not mention the fact that Mr. Gordon was not a railway man. He mentioned the fact that he did not belong to the Canadian National personnel. Neither did Sir Henry Thornton. Therefore I hope that when my hon. friend makes another pro-nunciamento he will not speak so much ex cathedra and will be broad enough to admit that there is possibly another point of view and that perhaps the point of view of the other fellow may not be so bad after all.

speechtext:
I wish to refer to the appointment for three or four minutes. There is no doubt about it that Mr. Donald Gordon did a great deal of useful work during the war and for a month or two afterwards in connection with the finance department. It was a Conservative government that established the Canadian National Railways as a national system many years ago, during 1919, 1920 and 1921. It proved to be a useful organization. There were two Vaughan brothers. The Vaughan family is an old family. In fact years ago when I was a very young alderman I sat with the father of Mr. Vaughan in the city council. One of the brothers went to the Canadian National Railways and performed a very useful public service. During the war he was overworked because of war work and many other activities. He dealt with many other economic conditions besides the railways and he rendered valuable service to the people of this country as president of the Canadian National Railways. His brother was one of the past presidents and head of Eaton's. It is well to remember that the principle of promotion might have been considered by the government, because I believe in the principle of promotion if you have a man with executive ability to take the place.
In the dark days of 1917 a royal commission was appointed to make a survey of the railway systems of this country. In this appointment one of the cardinal principles in the report of that commission is being violated. The Drayton commission consisted of Sir Henry Drayton, who was chairman of the board of railway commissioners at the time, Mr. A. H. Smith, who was president of the New York Central, and Mr. Acworth, a great British engineer, who during the war was head of a great system in England. He was a great railway man. It was said by the leaders of the government, the opposition, and others that Mr. Acworth was one of the greatest railway men of the great railways of the world. They were appointed to survey the railway system of this country, not only the C.N.R. but the other railways as well.
Canadian National Railways They reported to the government. What was their report? Their report said that there should be no appointment until it was agreed to by the railway commission.
In connection with this appointment, I think we might have tried to obtain a great British engineer. We tried three or four Americans before. They were all good presidents and did good work no doubt, but when we did not have a promotion in the ranks I believe we should have tried a great British engineer. We should have brought one out here. We should have tried an engineer who knew something about the war and war conditions in connection with the British railways. During the war over there they linked up all the various branches, which we have not got, and they performed useful service. I am sorry that the government did not consider that feature of it. That is all I have to say. No doubt Donald Gordon has been appointed by the financial powers. I wish him every success. I believe we would have been far better off if we had acted the way I proposed and got a British engineer. We should have tried one of that description to head this great national asset.

25.	Marketing service-dairy products, $594,077.

The hon. member for
Leeds mentioned the surplus supply of canned milk in that county. Could the Minister of Agriculture tell us what are the prospects for the marketing of evaporated milk, powdered milk and condensed milk?

That subject was discussed at considerable length the other evening, the question as to whether or not it is possible to market the butter-and I understand it is that to which the hon. member is referring.
I am referring to evaporated milk.

There are many different kinds of canned milk. I find that the stock of condensed milk at the beginning of 1948 stood at 2,654,000 pounds. The production during that year was 39,741,000 pounds. The exports amounted to 21,219,000 pounds and the domestic consumption was 17,587,000 pounds. The carryover at the end of the year amounted to 3,592,000 pounds.

That brings us down to the beginning of this year. Naturally we have not the figures yet for the end of the year, but we have figures down to the end of June. The total quantity of concentrated milk products manufactured in June was approximately 49,750,000 pounds, a decrease of 7 million pounds as compared with last year. Concentrated whole milk products declined to the extent of almost 7 million pounds, while milk by-products registered an increase of about 750,000 pounds. Evaporated milk, one of the most important of the whole milk products group, showed a decline of 4,500,000 pounds; and the production of skim milk powder, the leading skim milk product, declined 750,000 pounds.
The importance of those figures is that the production of all these milk products is on the decline. It may be argued by some that that is not a good thing. There are others however who would argue that, in the longtime interest of the dairy industry, it is not a bad thing to have the production of canned milk somewhat slowed down. The long-time planning and policy in connection with Canadian dairy farming has been that the surplus milk should go into the production of cheese. This has been due to a number of factors with which most members of the committee are familiar, and I do not feel I need discuss them this evening.
There are certain sections of Canada where it is most important, if they are to be able to carry on dairying effectively, that a very considerable quantity of milk be turned into cheese. There was a time, just at the end of the war, when it paid better to put milk in cans; and because it paid better to put milk in cans by far the greater part of the surplus over and above the whole-milk consumption and butter consumption went into cans. There was some difficulty in marketing the full amount of that production.
The result has been that the farmers have been delivering the milk to cheese factories rather than to canning factories in much greater quantities, and we are on the way back to producing greater quantities of cheese. I said in the discussion the other evening that, whereas we had entered into a contract with Great Britain at the beginning of this year to sell her 50 million pounds of cheese, no one who was preparing the statistics at that time thought we would be able to produce that amount, basing his estimates on the record of the last few years. But because of what I have just mentioned, namely the difficulty of marketing canned milk at the same price as that at which it had been marketed a year ago, the farmers turned over to cheese, with the result that at the end of

the season we had 10 million pounds more than we had contracted to sell to Great Britain.
I wish we had had a proper estimate at the beginning of the season, because I am satisfied that last December we could have sold that 10 million pounds of cheese to Britain. Had we known we were going to have 75 million pounds of cheese, we could have sold it. But since everyone who was compiling statistics and who was associated with the dairy industry in this country believed we could not produce more than 50 million pounds-indeed believed that we could not produce that much-we finally, in order to assist Britain in the matter of dealing with dollars in advance, said to her, "We will cut the contract down to 50 million pounds, because we think that is a little more than we are going to have".
This change in the balance between cheese and canned milk has put us back on the road we were trying to follow before, and which we found very difficult to follow, namely the process of producing cheese for the British market, which has always been available to us throughout the years, and which we believe will be available to us in the years ahead. And so now, when we are discussing a contract with Great Britain for the coming year, we are insisting upon raising rather than lowering the figures. I have an idea that we will get rid of the surplus of canned milk of one kind or another-and there are three or four different types of it. One would have to go over the figures for all of them to get the exact position.
I am of the opinion that we will be able to get rid of that canned milk to fairly good advantage, but indications are that we will not be able to get a return sufficiently high to induce people to stay away from the production of cheese. As I said a few minutes ago, I am not at all sure that that would be a bad thing for the dairy industry over a long period. It might be a good thing to encourage rather than discourage the transfer of more and more surplus milk into cheese.

During that transition period there would be 2,250 milk patrons in the county of Leeds who would not know which way to turn. The evaporated milk companies are still operating to the point where it is not economical for them to go ahead. They are building up every possible bit of storage and unless they are able to sell their stocks I do not know what is going to happen to the milk patrons. Through the years the number of cheese factories have diminished until, good as the factories are, they are simply not

able to look after the supply of milk available. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to getting rid of these surplus stocks that seem to be piling up beyond all reason.

26.	Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, and grants, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $1,201,923.

I understand that these subsidies are paid for storage plants at the processing and wholesaling levels rather than at the consumer or retail end. According to the details of the amounts to be paid out, it would appear that some areas will receive quite large subsidies while other areas will receive practically nothing. I notice that Quebec is to receive around $115,000; Ontario a little over $250,000; British Columbia some $400,000 while the total for the three prairie provinces will be a little less than $52,000. I am not complaining about the amounts to be received by any particular province, but I do want to point out that there is what I think is a real need for subsidies to locker plants in small towns, in particular on the prairies.
Many towns have inadequate train service during the winter months and it is impossible for the local merchants to bring in quantities of fresh fruits and vegetables. If an incentive were provided I am sure that a number of quick-freeze locker plants would be erected in the small localities. This would greatly improve the health of the people in the area and would provide a market throughout the year for perishable fruits and vegetables. I understand that there is some difficulty in finding a market for our fish. The farmers on the prairies would be glad to consume more Canadian fish if they could buy that wholesome product during the winter and place it in locker plants to be consumed during the summer. I submit that the minister and his officials should give serious consideration to extending this subsidy of thirty per cent to cover locker plants.

I think the Cold Storage Act dates back to 1907, which was long before we had the freezer plants that have been spoken of. The act provides that where a cold storage plant is made available to the public, whether it is under the control of an individual, of an operator or of a company, if it makes application before construction is started the government may agree to pay thirty per cent of the cost, half during the first year and the remainder being spread over the next three years.
I cannot recall an occasion when an application from Saskatchewan or Alberta has been refused. I think I am correct for
