Mr. Chairman, as a new member it is with a great deal of diffidence that I take the liberty of making a few remarks during the discussion of these estimates. As a farmer representing Anna-polis-Kings, which is essentially a rural constituency, I feel that I would be remiss in my duty not only to my constituents but also to this house, if I did not attempt to explain some things which are of vital importance to Annapolis-Kings. I hope they may be of considerable interest to all hon. members.
First, I should like to say how much the people of Annapolis-Kings appreciate the friendly and helpful attitude of the government to our problems. In particular, I should like to commend the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for their helpfulness during the past troublesome years. We particularly appreciate their splendid efforts in effecting a sale of Canadian apples to the United Kingdom this year.

Supply-Agriculture
Hon. members are probably aware that the Nova Scotia apple industry has been a war casualty since 1939. The financial support being given by the dominion and provincial governments to the marketing of Nova Scotia apples with a view to saving the industry will, I believe, be approved by the Canadian people generally. People will realize that the chief outlet for our apples in the United Kingdom has been lost through no fault of our own. When trees were set out in Nova Scotia which would produce the varieties most popular in Britain, there was every reason to believe that our crops would continue to be saleable in a stable and profitable market. With the loss of the British purchasing power, we now face the probability of being years without that profitable market.
In the meantime, attempts have been made to revamp our industry. Although we still talk in terms of barrels, there are four large modern cold storage plants in which standard boxes and crates are packed. There are also six smaller cold storage warehouses, and most of the common storage warehouses are now equipped to pack in containers other than barrels. Old trees and trees of unprofitable varieties are being removed. Much grafting into better varieties has been done, but there is still much to do. Each grower must now determine what he and his farm are best adapted to produce so that other products will be available to make up for the loss in fruit.
Last year's crop was a great disappointment. Starting with continuous wet weather in the spring and culminating in three severe frosts in October, while much of the abnormally small crop was still on the trees, the resultant returns to the growers were small. Thanks to the efforts of the Canadian government, this year a deal has been finalized whereby the British government will spend $1,500,000 for the purchase of Canadian apples. This is being matched by a like amount from the Canadian government. This is the type of assistance that many of the better growers have been hoping for, but unfortunately the prices being offered are too low to meet the high cost of production. Growers are naturally hopeful that they may be able to secure additional assistance to meet this year's expenses, and hope that such agreements may be finalized in the very near future.
To enlarge slightly on my statement-I shall try to be brief even at the risk of not making myself entirely clear-the sale price to Britain is based on 80 per cent of the price paid by the United Kingdom for Canadian apples in 1946. As there is a large crop of apples in the world today and we would all
[Mr. Elderkin.l
like to keep down the cost of living, this looked about right. Actually the price is not nearly enough to pay the cost of production. A large volume of apples not designated in the agreement with Britain, and which are not readily saleable on the domestic market, will also have to be taken into consideration. These will probably have to be sold to processors. The returns from these apples would vary from 60 cents for apples for vinegar to $2 per barrel for canning apples. With the exception of juice apples, warehouse expenses would be 25 to 50 cents per barrel, depending on the type of grading required for any particular processing job.
In 1948 the expenditure for spray material and fertilizer had increased two and one-half times over that of 1940. This year, there was again a marked increase in the cost of spray material and, to a lesser extent, in fertilizer. If the unit price of apples to Britain this year had been based on 100 per cent of our 1946 sales, we could probably have met the increased cost of production, but without any profit. This year's crop is not large, but it is much larger than last year's and the quality of the fruit is superior to any crop for the past several years. Having no wish to weary hon. members, I have not tried to be statistical, but merely to give a general outline in order that there might be a better appreciation of our problems.

Mr. Chairman, from what the hon. member has just said, I understand a deal has been made between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom for $3 million worth of apples. No doubt the minister negotiated this agreement. It is my understanding also that those apples are to be purchased in eastern Canada and western Canada. The minister knows that the constituency from which I come embraces the counties of Northumberland and Prince Edward, and is very good apple country. Would the minister be kind enough to explain to me, to my constituents and neighbours why the apples are not purchased in Ontario but from the other sections of the country? I am sure he has a good explanation. Would he care to answer that?

Mr. Chairman, the general position is that we have been trying to take care of the apple producers since 1939. I believe a fair job has been done and the producers will acknowledge that. In the first place, back in 1939, we started an attempt to arrange for the sale of the apple crop in Canada. In doing so, we found that the apple growers of Ontario and Quebec had exported very few apples. Most of their apples were sold in the central part of Canada.

In the first year, it was arranged that that market was not to be interfered with, except under permit. Then there was an attempt to deal with the surplus apples of Nova Scotia. Later on, the department was asked to deal with some of those of British Columbia as well, and we undertook to do that. As a result of entering into that arrangement at the beginning of the war, we have found it necessary to continue similar arrangements from that time until now. It was found as we went along that it was not necessary to have definite restrictions put upon the sale of apples out of the central provinces because all of the apples of the central provinces found a fairly ready market in the centres of those provinces; and it was found that in most years a considerable quantity of apples could be allowed to move from the maritime provinces to, say, Montreal and from British Columbia into cities right across eastern Canada. That was because of facts that I do not think it is necessary to discuss tonight any further than to recite them. But the general position was that each of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec was entitled pretty much to its own market as long as it could supply it, and when it could not supply it these apples came in from other parts of Canada. The prairie provinces were left entirely to British Columbia.
Nova Scotia, which produces most of the apples in the maritimes, found it extremely difficult to find a market anywhere except to the extent that they were allowed to get into the central part of Canada, or in case we could arrange a market for their apples in the United States or, as we did for a few years during the war, arrange a market for the greater part of their product in Great Britain. We were able to do that during most of the years of the war, but when we got down to the end of the war we found it even more difficult than during the war itself to obtain a market in Great Britain. On a previous occasion I recited the reasons for that fact, and it probably would only excite some political discussion if I were to recite them again tonight, so I shall save it for another occasion.
Nevertheless, we did get into the position last year where we took over 200,000 barrels of Nova Scotia apples. At one time we thought it might be a good thing to give the apples away. Some exception was taken to that course, so we put some of the apples in cans and dehydrated some of them. Finally we sold all of those apples that we could sell. Then when we found that we could not sell any more, we advertised right across Canada, in all the charitable organizations of the country and in hospitals, the fact that we had these apples and were prepared to provide
Supply-Agriculture
them free of cost other than, I think, the freight to have them shipped to those institutions. We finally disposed of the apples in that way at a cost to the government. I just recite these facts in order to show that the central part of Canada has not been left entirely out of the picture. We have kept the surplus apples off the market until such time as they have had an opportunity to supply any market that there is. We have not even given apples away until it was found that the position had been fairly well taken care of in so far as the purchases of apples were concerned. We now come down to this year.
Britain did not want any apples. I was over there in January and told them about the hundreds of thousands of trees that had been pulled out because they could not buy the apples. I must say that that statement obtained more circulation in the press of Great Britain than anything else I had ever said in that country. They thought it was a rather difficult position to see Canadians in, after what they had done during the war, where they were compelled to pull out hundreds of thousands of trees simply because the British could not take the apples. The Minister of Trade and Commerce went over there a little later and was able to prevail upon them to put $1,500,000 into buying, as they thought in the beginning, Nova Scotia apples. I do not think they had in mind any other apples at the time they were talking first, largely because of the story that had been circulated with regard to pulling out trees and doing all these things to try to suit our position to the new developments. They agreed to that, conditional upon our putting $1,500,000 into the purchase of apples too.
The people of Nova Scotia are still asking us to do for their apple crop this year something similar to what we have done in other years. We suggested to them that we thought, before discussing that question, that they ought to take part of the offer the British had made. The British offered to take $1,500,000 worth of those apples at 80 per cent of the 1946 price. They said they thought the price had been too high last year, that it had been too high the year before, and that the price which was being asked this year was too high; but they said they were prepared to take $1,500,000 worth at 80 per cent of the 1946 price. As will be recalled, that was the year when Britain took a considerable part of the apple crop of the maritimes and of British Columbia.
We discussed the matter with the apple producers of Nova Scotia and suggested that we thought that it would not be a bad thing, from the point of view either of the present or of future possibilities of marketing apples

in Great Britain, if they would accept the offer at 80 per cent of the 1946 price. They went home with that intention. Now I understand that, when they examined into the varieties that they had, it is true to say that they have not been prepared up to now to undertake to supply this season the total quantity of apples that the British are prepared to take from them. They are reserving the right to decide later on a certain proportion of the amount that is required. British Columbia has agreed to take up its proportion of the apples, and to ship at the prices that have been indicated. I understand that in the area that is spoken of, down around Northumberland, they feel that they would like to fill part of this contract. Up to now it has not been indicated to us that Nova Scotia is prepared to provide them all. I think there must be some limitation upon the time during which they will be required to provide them; and if they are not prepared to provide the remainder of the quantity at the price which is indicated, and if there are others elsewhere in Canada who are prepared to put the apples up at those prices, I think the government would be in duty bound to accept their offer to do so and to see to it that the apples are sent forward. That is the present position in relation to the matter.
I wish to say without any hesitation that we are desirous of getting out of the apple business just as fast as we can. We have said to the people of Nova Scotia: If you can sell your apples at a price which is sufficiently good to make it unnecessary for you to accept this British offer, then we are not so sure that you are having any great difficulty in marketing your apples. When I look at the figures which indicate that we are eating in Canada now more apples than we marketed altogether inside and outside of Canada in the last year before the war, I am beginning to think that there may be something in their contention that they can sell their apples to better advantage in Canada than they can by sending them to Britain under the offer that Britain has made. And I would be a little afraid that, if that is true of Nova Scotia, it will be true of Ontario as well, and perhaps more so, and we may find it a little difficult to get apples at those prices.

The minister has clearly explained the situation with regard to apples being purchased by Britain and the apples being paid for by the Canadian government and going to England. He will remember

that for some years the British government refused to accept gift apples unless consigned direct to the ministry of food. A few days ago I saw some report in the press of a change in that situation whereby they would accept from the producer organization or grower organization apples consigned direct to the consumer in Great Britain. Can the minister explain to the house what the situation is at the present time?

This latter matter of boxes going from others to the government is just individual to individual. If any hon. member desires to send a box of apples over to a friend in Britain he would be permitted to do so, but that is not a matter-
The British have agreed to that.
Yes; but it is not a matter of providing apples to the trade direct if they are a gift, and the $1,500,000 worth of Canadian apples to all intents and purposes is a gift.
Did I understand the minister to say that the Canadian government has in fact provided $1,500,000 and the British government $1,500,000, making $3 million in all?

Yes, but the British government have agreed to take their $1,500,000 first, and as they are being delivered they are paying for them. From there on the Canadian government will be paying for whatever apples are purchased, and they have agreed to purchase all the $1,500,000, provided the apples are offered at the price.
Is the price paid by the Canadian government based upon the 1946 price?
Yes, the same price.
From all parts of Canada?

The present arrangement is from the maritimes and Nova Scotia largely and from British Columbia. Definite amounts are set, but, as I indicated a few moments ago, the Nova Scotians are not sure that they want to provide all the quantity that has been allotted to them, in which case we have said to other parts of Canada: if you want to supply them at the price, that will be possible.

I should like to touch on another aspect of the fruit and vegetable matter. It has nothing to do with the point which has just been discussed. As the minister well knows, the lifting of the import restrictions on many classifications of fresh fruits and vegetables coming into Canada, which was announced by the Minister of Finance not so very long ago, has a direct bearing and may have a material effect upon the future of some of our growers. I mention

that only for this particular reason, namely, to emphasize a point which is very often brought to my attention by the growers in my section of the country. I refer specifically to what is commonly known as the dumping duties on the tail end of the United States surplus produce coming into this country and competing with the initial period of the market for many of our crops. In view of the fact that this is one of the delicate subjects that growers from time to time find on their doorsteps, perhaps the government might give consideration to it. I know that the minister himself does not actually set the time limit and the timing of the application of the dumping duties on the imports of Unijed States fruits and vegetables, but his department does have an important part to play, together with the recommendation of the growers and others, in the timing. I should like to emphasize this one fact, because since the import restrictions have been lifted the necessity becomes greater than ever before to protect the growers when the first part of their crop is about to be marketed, particularly in the spring or in other times of the year. As the minister knows, from time to time there has been a disposition to allow the United States stuff to spill over onto the market which our growers feel should be theirs at the beginning of their season. The minister and the committee will readily agree that many of our growers of fresh fruits and vegetables find that the early part of their market is their best market, and for that reason it is that much more essential that that period should be protected. The complaint, which no doubt the minister and many of us who come from fruit and vegetable areas receive, is that when the time is set for the dumping duties to operate an immense amount of rolling stock is on its way here and in the first period of the marketing season of our own fresh fruits and vegetables the United States stuff, which is surplus very largely, is dumped upon our markets to the detriment of our own producers. There has been a disposition to work out a reasonable solution of the problem. When they are not in a position to serve the domestic market in Canada with many of these delicious fresh foods our growers may not have objected quite so strenuously to the market being taken care of in other ways, but they do seriously object when they themselves are able to fill the market, and particularly in the first part of their producing season. At that time they do seriously object to the United States surplus being dumped on the market, thereby spoiling what would otherwise be a very good market for many of the growers. What my argument is attempting to buttress is this. In some instances there ought to be a little
Supply-Agriculture
earlier application of the dumping duties on some of the fresh fruits and vegetables. I make these remarks in a general way because I do not want to take up the time of the committee except to urge the government to review the situation very carefully. In view of the import restrictions having been lifted, my argument becomes more forceful in regard to the point I am trying to make, and that is, an earlier application of the dumping duties to enable our growers to get the best advantage of the early part of the market for their produce.

I should like to say one word. The term "dumping duties", as the hon. member for Peel will understand, is not usually applied to this particular operation. There is a dumping duty provided for in the act which operates automatically with regard to different products. We have usually called these seasonal duties. They are put on for the purpose of regulating the coming onto this market of fruits and vegetables largely from the United States at a time just prior to the coming onto the market of Canadian products, at a time, as has been suggested, when the fruits and vegetables coming from farther south are at the tail end of their season.
There is no act that is administered by the different departments that is more carefully administered than this particular one. The initial action is taken by the horticultural association in indicating when they desire to have certain things done. That is then checked by the department concerned; and, as has been said, the Department of Agriculture has a great deal to do with setting dates when the act comes into operation in connection with certain vegetables or fruits. That is all done most carefully. The hon. member said he did not think that the minister had much to do with it. As a matter of fact the minister had nearly everything to do with it up to a certain point, and the minister finally said that he did not think he had the time to examine into all of these matters in the manner in which they should be examined into, and insisted upon some others doing that particular job. I must admit now that I do not do as much of the work in connection with it as was done by the minister at one time, but I do not think it means that it is done any less efficiently than it was done before. I had an idea that it would be done more efficiently if it were done in the manner in which it is done now. I have had little, if any, complaint about it during the time it was in operation. It is true that while the special provision that shut out certain American fruits and vegetables altogether was on it was not necessary for the act to operate. Now that that has been

done away with, the other act does operate. The greatest of care will be taken in deciding upon the dates.

Perhaps honey would fall under this item. It would be interesting to the committee and the country if the minister would tell us the situation with respect to honey this year, in somewhat the same manner that he told us about the government's operations in apples. My recollection is that last year there was a surplus to the extent of several million pounds of honey. The matter was so serious that the government was forced to place a floor price under it. As I recall-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-I believe that price was thirteen cents a pound.
Would the minister give some information in regard to that operation? For example, what loss to the government was involved, if any; and what is the situation this year in connection with a possible surplus on the market?

Last year it was represented to us that there was a surplus of 5 million pounds of honey on the Canadian market. Statistics presented to us by the honey producers led us to believe that that was correct. The question was discussed in the house last session and was also discussed with the government. Finally the government decided, and the announcement was made to the house, that we were prepared to provide funds sufficient to purchase 5 million pounds of honey in surplus supply, and to take it off the Canadian market for the time being with a view to finding a market elsewhere for it.
The fact is that we were never able to find more than 3 million pounds. We did buy that amount at prices ranging from 10 to 13 cents a pound. As this honey is pasteurized it will keep. We know that this year the producers have a short crop, and it will require the whole 3 million pounds-and probably we could use a little more-to supply the market with honey this year. So that there is no problem in connection with that. It is simply a matter of our having taken off last year's market 3 million pounds of honey, carrying it over to this year. Now we are able to put it back on the market to increase the short supply produced this year.
Had the drought something to do with that?
Yes, it had a great deal to do with it.

Is it correct that last year the growers of raspberries and strawberries were threatened with penalties by the
[Mr. Gardiner.)
states of Oregon and Washington in which state legislation was proposed whereby we would not be able to ship our produce to those states; and is it a fact that we took steps pointing out to them that we purchased from those states and that in turn we should be allowed to make deliveries to them?
My information is that the legislation passed last year by the state of Washington along the lines suggested by the hon. member was later rescinded.
That is right.

That was due to the fact that, after representations from British Columbia, the government here in Ottawa made representations to the Capitol at Washington, and they in turn made representations to the state of Washington as a result of which the legislation was rescinded. I am not aware of any legislation put forward this year.
No, I do not think there is any.
If there were any further difficulties, they would meet with similar treatment.

28. Marketing service-livestock and livestock products, $1,113,750.

I notice there is an increase in the vote for the administration of this item. What new arrangements have been made with reference to the marketing of raw furs this year? Are we going to adopt a system similar to what we had last year, one which was not too successful so far as the producer is concerned?
This industry was cruelly treated by the late government in matters of taxation, and it took out of the industry, through taxes large sums of money-so much indeed that it drove the industry almost into bankruptcy.
What do you mean by "the late government"?

Just you keep quiet. Now that times have changed a little, I suggest the government should adopt a different system of grading. Does it intend to drive the industry off the face of the earth altogether? Four years ago this country was producing 285,000 silver fox skins; today production will be down below 45,000. There should be an advantage in the market, when there is no surplus.
We got 182 skins this year.

If there is going to be a surplus, we want to know how these skins are

going to be marketed. I see a provision here for two graders, one of whom receives $4,000 or $5,000 and the other $3,000 or $4,000. That is all right, but the government is making the grade so exclusive and so high that no producer today, unless he is producing the very top from all his animals, can get anywhere near the cost of feed and wages from the sale of the furs.
It is time we had some consideration, because it is only a few years ago the government was warned that because of the unjust taxation they were placing upon raw furs they were driving the industry out of production altogether. They had a process tax on the raw article, and then on top of that a sales tax. These were the most unjust forms of taxation ever perpetrated upon any product of the farm.
There is now an opportunity for the government to look into the marketing of furs. If the government is going to give assistance to the fur producers by way of subsidy, let it subsidize sales so that the producers will receive at least the cost of production. That can be done by putting in a grading system whereby they will not grade against the price of the article, but rather grade the article as it is needed on the market.
I say the minister should give these people an opportunity to come back and receive some of the money taken from them by taxation, so they may be established once again and kept in business. I would ask that the minister give this matter some consideration.

Perhaps the minister
would answer a question at this time about the marketing of poultry products. In December of this year the Anglo-Canadian contract for poultry products expires. It looks as though the production will be increased in 1950 and we will need a market for something like 400 million dozen eggs in all forms. A total of 350 million dozen eggs will be produced this year of which, as I said before, 46 million dozen will be shipped to the mother country.
I know the minister is concerned about the marketing of our egg products and I wonder if he could give us some assurance that this market will be maintained next year?

Mr. Chairman, as has been stated during the war, we did develop a
Supply-Agriculture
market in Great Britain for nur eggs. In the year before the war we marketed one million dozen eggs in Britain. But at the peak during the war or at the end of the war we marketed 83 million dozen. Part of those were marketed as shell or fresh eggs, part as storage eggs and part as dried or frozen eggs.
About 24 months ago we were just at the peak of supplying the British market. It is true that the year before last the British came over and suggested that they would have difficulty in taking all our eggs, but they finally entered into a contract to take them last year. Then last year they came over and suggested that they could get along without our eggs. It was not a case of their not wanting them, it was not a case of there not being a market there, it was a case of their trying to determine where they might spend the limited amount of dollars that they had.
They said that they could get eggs from other places, or at least supplies which would permit them to get along without ours. At that time we indicated to them that we would have some difficulty in meeting their wishes in that regard. In that regard I must emphasize to the committee that our position in relation to the British has not been quite what it has been pictured throughout the country.
The British have come to us with a problem. They have said that they found it difficult to get enough dollars with which to buy in Canada all the things they would like to buy. We have told them that we could scarcely be expected to ask our people to take lower returns and could scarcely be expected to feed a nation of much greater numbers of people than we have unless we could receive some return.
We told them that we were prepared to try to find a market for what they were not able to take and pay for. As has been indicated in this discussion, in some cases where we have failed to find a market for a product, such as apples, we have provided some of the product to them at our own cost. But we have avoided that as much as we could recently. In connection with eggs, we told them that we thought we could find a market for all of our shell eggs in Canada or the United States, that we could induce our people to eat a few more and be careful when marketing in the United States to do so without causing any difficulty.
If we just said to our producers that they could ship all the eggs they wished to the United States probably most of those eggs would find their way to border cities like Detroit, Buffalo and a few other places. Then there would be trouble with the producers in the vicinity of those particular cities. Instead of doing that, our people went down to cities like St. Louis and other points in the centre

of the United States away from the boundary and made arrangements for our fresh eggs to be delivered to those interior points.
We had expected to sell far more eggs in the United States on that basis than we did. We could have sold far more eggs but the eggs were not available to be sold. In other words, that quantity of eggs, which the British were not required to take and which we thought we could sell on this and the United States market, we did not have to supply to any market.
I am not blaming anybody for that. I think our producers, whether of eggs or of any other product, look at the whole position and try to meet the situation as they find it to their best advantage. I presume that they handled their position in a manner which was satisfactory.
When it came to dried eggs we insisted on the British taking the 46 million dozen which we estimated at that time could be produced in that form. The British agreed to take them but it would appear at the moment that we probably will not supply more than 34 million dozen.
I merely cite this in order to say to people who are always talking about our having lost markets, about our not being able to find markets for our products, that one of our difficulties has been that we have not been able to find the product to put on the market. There is a good reason for that. Something was said about grading furs. This does not apply in just the same way to furs as it does to eggs. You can soon get eggs into a position where nobody wants to eat them, and it is not so many years ago that that was the position in this country. But we undertook to grade all eggs that were going on the market and in a few years we doubled the consumption in Canada per head of population. We have gone on to increase that from time to time by getting out a product that everyone is desirous of eating.
To answer the last part of the hon. member's question, may I say that we are attempting to make a contract with the British. We hope to make one that will take
care of any surplus we may have. We are hopeful that when these contracts are made our people will put forth an effort to see that the product is produced to supply the market. I do not think anyone up to now is contending that the price range on all these products in the last few years has not been fairly good. If it has been fairly good, and if we want to market more products in the markets that are available, then I think we ought to produce them and put them on the market.

I know the minister feels sure that our farmers would like to be assured that there will be a market for 1950. Does the minister feel in his own mind that there will be a substantial market in 1950 for poultry products?

Nothing has happened which would indicate that it will be in any respect different from what it has been in the past year, and we did find markets for more than they were able to produce.
